articles.title: Scope WebMCP Tools to the Open React Workflow
articles.description: On the Events list, the browser discovered zero WebMCP tools. Opening an event draft exposed four....
articles.body_html:
On the Events list, the browser discovered zero WebMCP tools. Opening an event draft exposed four. Switching to a trip draft replaced them with five trip tools.

That route sequence is the behavior I wanted when Trip Workbench gained a second workflow. Registering every operation at startup would have exposed two unrelated domains even when only one editor was visible.

Page-scoped tools make the current context clearer. They also create a design question: how does an agent enter a workflow whose tools exist only after the right page is open?

Keep domain identity in the contract

The event editor has a title, date range, time zone, location mode, location label, and notes. The trip editor has airports, travel dates, cabin, traveler count, and purpose.

Both workflows reuse authorization, revision, and command-receipt patterns, but they keep separate coordinators, services, tables, validation rules, policy versions, and identifiers. Event tools accept eventId; trip tools accept draftId.

The event editor exposes:

Tool Purpose
get_event_draft Read saved fields, revision, status, and unsaved-change state
update_event_draft Apply an allowed patch to an expected revision
validate_event_draft Return field issues and policy findings
prepare_event_review Show findings while the event remains a draft

This synthetic example does not send invitations, connect to calendars, or book venues.

Register when the editor has context

The React editor registers tools only after it has a draft identity and status. A condensed lifecycle looks like this:

useEffect(() => {
  if (!eventId || draftStatus !== "draft") return;

  const registration = new AbortController();

  registerEventDraftTools({
    eventId,
    canMutate: Boolean(canMutate),
    coordinator: eventCoordinator,
    signal: registration.signal,
    onStatus: setRegistration,
  });

  return () => registration.abort();
}, [eventId, draftStatus, canMutate, eventCoordinator]);

Chrome’s current imperative API documents this signal-based lifecycle. As of Chrome 153, aborting the registration removes the tool without cancelling an already-running execution. That is helpful for component cleanup, but it means route cleanup and in-flight operation safety are separate responsibilities.

The draft identity belongs in the dependency list. React may retain the same component type while moving from one event to another; the old tools must disappear and the new handlers must bind to the new event.

Test the exact route sequence

The native browser run signed in normally, used visible navigation, created a synthetic event draft, and inspected the browser’s real tool collection. It did not call the coordinator directly.

Context Discovered interface
Traveler on Trips list none
Traveler on Events list none
Traveler editing an event four event tools
Traveler editing a trip five trip tools
Traveler back on Events list none
Traveler reopening the event four event tools
Observer editing the event read, validate, prepare
Observer back on Events list none

An exact-name assertion catches stale registrations:

const expected = [
  "get_event_draft",
  "prepare_event_review",
  "update_event_draft",
  "validate_event_draft",
];

const actual = page.webmcp.tools()
  .map((tool) => tool.name)
  .sort();

assert.deepEqual(actual, expected);

The observer result is useful but limited. Omitting a mutation tool reduces accidental exposure; it does not authorize anything. The server must still reject writes from an actor without permission.

Execute a useful operation, not just discovery

Tool names alone do not prove that the page contract works. The run updated a synthetic workshop, validated it, and prepared an inline review.

{
  "title": "Customer engineering workshop",
  "startDate": "2026-11-25",
  "endDate": "2026-11-26",
  "timeZone": "America/Los_Angeles",
  "locationMode": "manual",
  "locationLabel": "Demo workshop room",
  "notes": "Synthetic example; no invitations"
}

The accepted update moved the draft from revision 1 to 2. prepare_event_review displayed a MANUAL_LOCATION requirement with canSubmit: true and submitted: false. The visible title matched an independent database query, and the event remained a draft with zero submissions.

The injected test clock was October 14, 2026, so the dates were still in the future. Pinning time matters when validation depends on dates.

A narrow interface needs a way in

The Events list intentionally exposes no editor tools, so those tools cannot open their own workflow.

The recorded run used the normal Events link and “New event draft” button. A browser agent with navigation and actuation can take a similar path. A client limited to WebMCP calls cannot.

There are two defensible designs:

  1. Treat browser navigation as part of the client contract.
  2. Add a bounded list-level tool to open an authorized draft or create a new one.

I would avoid a generic “call any API” or “run arbitrary JavaScript” escape hatch. It destroys the narrow schemas and server checks that make the editor tools reviewable.

Do not turn tool count into a performance claim

This run proves that the discovered interface changes with route and role. It does not prove that a model completes tasks faster with four tools than with nine.

That requires a separate evaluation: keep the task and executable behavior fixed, vary the visible tool set, and measure wrong-target updates, workflow-entry failures, correct persisted outcomes, recovery steps, and final-answer accuracy.

The current evidence supports a narrower conclusion: expose editing tools where the relevant object is visible, remove them when the context ends, preserve server authorization, and design an explicit entry path for the clients you actually support.

articles.title: I Replaced $3,000 Eye-Trackers with a Laptop Webcam: Building a Hands-Free Spatial Communicator with SmartSpectra
articles.description: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge           What I Built   Traditional...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge

What I Built

Traditional Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) systems for people with severe motor and speech impairments (such as ALS, high-level quadriplegia, or locked-in syndrome) force an impossible trade-off: spend $3,000+ on specialized infrared eye-tracking hardware, or endure exhausting dwell-time interfaces where staring at a button for 1,000 ms just to register a single click leads to rapid visual fatigue and constant accidental selections (the classic "Midas Touch" problem).

Worse, existing gaze communicators suffer from two real-world bedside failures that nobody talks about:

  1. Attention Theft: The screen holds the user's eyes hostage. If they glance up to make eye contact with a loved one or try to vocalize, the cursor misfires and types gibberish.
  2. One-Sided Visibility: Caregivers and family members standing across the room can't read a laptop screen facing the patient.

NeuroScribe Studio turns any standard consumer webcam into a responsive, spatial assistive communication console by decoupling targeting from activation, introducing conversational standby gating, and syncing messages in real time to a Caregiver Partner HUD (/partner).

Core Capabilities

  • 3D Spatial Gaze & Head-Pose Targeting: High-contrast, multi-level hierarchical communication boards (Physical Needs, Comfort & Position, People & Care, Quick Dialogue, Expressions, Emergency) driven by smoothed iris vectors and head pitch/yaw.
  • Temporal Blink Discrimination: A client-side state machine separates natural involuntary blinks (< 250 ms, ignored) from deliberate selection blinks (350–850 ms, confirms card) and extended closures (> 1,200 ms, undo/backspace).
  • Attentive Standby Lockout: Automatically freezes card inputs the instant face.talking is detected or the user tilts their head up (pitch > 14°) to make natural eye contact with a caregiver.
  • Interactive 5-Second Calibration: Dynamically normalizes iris bounding thresholds (minX, maxX, minY, maxY) and blink timing windows to adapt to different seating angles, wheelchair heights, and eyelid control speeds.
  • Cross-Device Caregiver Mirror (/partner): Real-time WebSocket sync broadcasts composed phrases, spoken audio chimes, and haptic vibration alerts (navigator.vibrate) to a caregiver's smartphone across the room—complete with two-way acknowledgment back to the patient.
  • Human-in-the-Loop Speech Synthesis: Messages are never spoken automatically; users review their constructed sentence and confirm [Speak Aloud] to trigger the browser's native Web Speech API.

Demo

What Happens in the Demo:

  1. Consent & Privacy Gate: Explicit pre-capture authorization explaining local in-memory processing and zero telemetry.
  2. Hands-Free Spatial Navigation: Navigating the 3D spatial wave-cards via eye gaze and selecting phrases with deliberate blinks—with hands completely off the keyboard.
  3. Attentive Standby Lockout: Looking up and speaking freezes the grid so natural eye contact with a caregiver never causes accidental selections.
  4. Caregiver Mirror Sync (/partner): Confirming Speak Aloud broadcasts the message in real time to a second device with audio and haptic feedback.

Code

  • Public GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Akulbanxal/Neuroscribe

How It Responds to Human Signals

Rather than treating SmartSpectra as a passive telemetry display, NeuroScribe Studio orchestrates four live Presage human signals in real time to power a hands-free, zero-fatigue assistive communication loop:

  1. Iris Vectors & 478 Facial Landmarks (faceMetrics) → Spatial Card Targeting & 3D Parallax:

    • Normalized iris coordinates ([0, 1]) and head pose (pitch and yaw) are streamed from the local SmartSpectra Node SDK daemon (@smartspectra/node-sdk) at 30 FPS over WebSockets (ws://localhost:8080).
    • To eliminate raw webcam jitter, the frontend applies an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) filter (α = 0.28–0.35) and maps the smoothed gaze vector onto calibrated 3×2 spatial wave-cards with deadzones, dynamically tilting the 3D glass deck in response to head orientation.

  2. Binary Blink Detection (face.blinking) → Temporal Selection & Undo State Machine:

    • Instead of exhausting dwell-time timers (staring at a button for 1,000+ ms), NeuroScribe measures the exact duration of continuous face.blinking.detected windows on the client side:
      • Natural involuntary blinks (< 250 ms): Ignored completely to prevent accidental clicks.
      • Deliberate selection blinks (350–850 ms): Fills a live neon progress bar on the targeted card and appends the phrase to the sentence builder.
      • Extended eye closure (> 1,200 ms): Triggers an instant Undo / Backspace action.

  3. Speech Articulation Detection (face.talking) & Head Pitch → Attentive Standby Lockout:

    • The moment face.talking.detected flips to true—or when the user lifts their chin (pitch > 14°) to make natural eye contact with a bedside caregiver—the UI immediately enters Attentive Standby, freezing all card selections and dimming the grid so real-world conversation never triggers false inputs.

  4. Respiratory Waveform (breathing.upperTrace) & Facial Expressions (faceMetrics.expressions) → Live HUD & Ambient Feedback:

    • Real-time upper-chest respiratory excursions drive the rhythmic breathing sparkline in the system status bar, while dominant facial expression probabilities subtly adapt the ambient spatial lighting.

SDK Integration Architecture

  • Backend Bridge (server.mjs): Initializes SmartSpectraSDK locally via C++ FFI with requestedMetrics: [...faceMetrics, ...breathingMetrics] and enableTelemetry: false, normalizing all frame timestamps to epoch microseconds (Date.now() * 1000) to guarantee continuous, stall-free streaming.
  • Frontend Consumer (useBiometrics.ts): Ingests the 30 FPS WebSocket JSON stream, applies EMA coordinate smoothing, runs the temporal blink discriminator, and synchronizes confirmed phrases to both the Web Speech API (speechSynthesis) and the cross-device Caregiver Mirror (/partner).

Prize Categories

I am entering NeuroScribe Studio for Best Thoughtful Real-World Use (Primary) as well as Best Overall Human-Sensing Experience.

Best Thoughtful Real-World Use

  • The Real-World Need: Millions of individuals living with severe motor and speech impairments—such as ALS, high-level spinal cord injuries, cerebral palsy, or brainstem stroke—lose the ability to speak or use touchscreens. Existing Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) setups either cost $3,000+ for dedicated infrared hardware or rely on exhausting dwell-time timers (staring at a button for 1,000+ ms to click) that cause rapid ocular fatigue and constant accidental inputs.
  • Who It’s For: Non-speaking or motor-impaired individuals who need a reliable, zero-cost way to express urgent needs, comfort adjustments, and everyday thoughts using only a standard laptop webcam—alongside their bedside caregivers and family members who need immediate visibility across the room.
  • How It Was Designed for Real-World Usability:
    • Zero-Fatigue Temporal Blink Activation: Decouples eye-gaze targeting from intentional blink confirmation (350–850 ms), ignoring involuntary natural blinks (< 250 ms) and mapping extended closures (> 1,200 ms) to Undo.
    • Attentive Standby Lockout: Automatically freezes card inputs when face.talking is detected or when the user tilts their head up (pitch > 14°) to make natural eye contact with a loved one—eliminating accidental selections during real-world conversation.
    • 5-Second Adaptive Calibration & High-Contrast Spatial Cards: Large, unmistakable 3×2 wave-cards with customizable blink thresholds and seating calibration accommodate varying wheelchair angles and eyelid control speeds.
    • Cross-Device Caregiver Mirror (/partner): Broadcasts composed phrases, spoken audio chimes, and haptic vibrations (navigator.vibrate) to a caregiver's smartphone in real time, complete with two-way acknowledgment back to the patient.

Consent and Data Handling

NeuroScribe Studio was architected from the ground up with strict privacy-first guardrails and full compliance with the challenge rules:

  • Explicit Pre-Capture Consent: Camera access and WebSocket biometric streaming remain completely disabled at launch until the user explicitly reviews and accepts the on-screen Camera Consent & Privacy Notice Modal (with a one-click option to revoke/pause capture at any time).
  • 100% Local In-Memory Processing (Zero Storage / Zero Sharing): Video frames are captured locally by the Node.js daemon (@smartspectra/node-sdk), processed strictly in volatile RAM, and immediately discarded. Zero video frames, facial images, landmark recordings, or biometric logs are ever saved to disk, persisted in databases, or transmitted to external servers.
  • Retention & Deletion: Because all processing occurs ephemerally in volatile memory with zero disk persistence, data retention is 0 seconds—nothing is stored, so no residual user data ever remains after closing the session.
  • SDK Telemetry Disabled: The SmartSpectra SDK instance is explicitly initialized with enableTelemetry: false, ensuring no diagnostic session telemetry or usage metrics leave the local machine.
  • No Third-Party Cloud AI Services: All gaze smoothing, blink classification, sentence assembly, and text-to-speech synthesis (window.speechSynthesis) run 100% locally on the user's device without calling external AI APIs.
  • Non-Medical & Non-Diagnostic Disclosure: NeuroScribe Studio is strictly an assistive human-computer interaction (HCI) communication interface. It makes no medical, diagnostic, or treatment claims, performs no clinical decision-making, and does not enable covert or non-consensual monitoring.

Agent Session

Built solo using React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and @smartspectra/node-sdk, with AI-assisted architectural iteration and UI prototyping.

articles.title: nginx 1.31's json_set directive rejects a bad webhook payload about 13 times faster than forwarding it
articles.description: I measured nginx 1.31's new native JSON parser against a Python backend doing the same validation: roughly 13x faster per-request rejection at low concurrency, half a backend's request count removed outright in a 50/50 mix, and no measurable overhead when nothing gets rejected at all.
articles.body_html:
A webhook receiver I built a few years ago always worked the same way: nginx took the connection, nginx forwarded the body, and the application decided whether the payload was junk. nginx 1.31.5 adds a module that lets nginx make that decision itself, by reading fields out of the JSON body before the request ever reaches a location block. I wanted to know what that was actually worth, not just what the changelog implied.

The module is ngx_http_json_module, built with --with-http_json_module (it's compiled into the official Docker image, but not into Ubuntu's 24.04 nginx apt package, which still ships 1.24.0). It adds one directive that matters, json_set, plus a depth limit. Alongside it, 1.31.5 also shipped predicate locations (location $variable) and client_body_early_read, which together let a location match be decided by the request body instead of only the URI.

I pulled nginx:1.31.8 (the current mainline patch, released 21 October 2026) and built the smallest realistic case: a webhook endpoint that only wants two event types, payment.created and payment.failed, and should reject everything else without bothering the application.

The setup

Old way, everything proxied through:

server {
    listen 18090;
    location / {
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Connection "";
        proxy_pass http://backend;
    }
}

New way, rejecting at the edge:

client_body_early_read 1;
json_set $event_type $request_body event.type;
map $event_type $is_invalid_event {
    "payment.created" 0;
    "payment.failed"  0;
    default           1;
}
server {
    listen 18091;
    location $is_invalid_event {
        return 400 "unknown event type\n";
    }
    location / {
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Connection "";
        proxy_pass http://backend;
    }
}

The backend is a small threaded Python server that parses the same JSON and returns 400 for anything that isn't one of the two valid event types, so both paths enforce the identical rule. I ran everything on loopback, no Docker network between containers, --network host so there's no extra hop to argue about.

What it actually saved

I sent 200 requests, alternating valid and invalid payloads, through each config and counted how many reached the backend:

requests sent reached backend
old way (run 1/2/3) 200 200 / 200 / 200
new way (run 1/2/3) 200 100 / 100 / 100

Every single invalid request was turned away at nginx. The backend never saw it. That's the entire point of the feature in one table: it's not about nginx being faster at HTTP, it's about deciding which requests are worth a backend's time before spending any.

The headline number

At concurrency 1, no contention, I measured the time to reject (or round-trip and reject) 1,000 invalid payloads, three times each:

run old way (round trip) new way (rejected at nginx)
1 1,840 req/s 25,780 req/s
2 2,006 req/s 21,862 req/s
3 1,775 req/s 25,153 req/s

Averaged, that's about 1,874 req/s against 24,265 req/s — roughly 13 times faster to say no. That gap is real and it isn't contention-related, since there's only one request in flight at a time either way. It's the cost of a TCP round trip and a Python thread versus a variable lookup.

The opposite reading

The obvious question is what this costs you when there's nothing to reject. I ran 3,000 all-valid requests through both configs, serially, three times:

run old way new way
1 1,729 req/s 1,680 req/s
2 1,578 req/s 1,688 req/s
3 1,572 req/s 1,574 req/s

That's noise, not a trend. I expected json_set plus the extra map lookup to cost something on every request even when nothing gets rejected, and I couldn't find it. At a 5% invalid mix the new way was consistently about 11-13% faster even though 95% of requests still had to go all the way to the backend either way, which argues the parsing cost is genuinely small relative to a real round trip.

Under concurrency, the comparison stops being fair

At 10 concurrent clients sending nothing but junk, old way managed 1,433 req/s; new way did 86,046. At 100 concurrent clients, old way dropped to 49 req/s with 3 failed requests, while new way stayed above 109,000 with none. I'm not reporting that ratio as nginx being thousands of times faster than a backend in general — it's what happens when a single-process, thread-per-connection Python server gets saturated by a flood of requests it has to accept, parse and reject one at a time. Hit directly with no proxy in front, that same backend topped out around 2,500 req/s at concurrency 50. The real finding isn't the multiplier, it's that under load the backend's own capacity becomes the thing junk traffic eats into, and removing it from that path removes the exposure entirely rather than just making it faster.

What the docs claim, checked

The module docs say a JSON document "is parsed only once per request, on the first access to any variable extracted from it, no matter how many variables are extracted." I tested that by extracting one field against extracting five fields from the same request body, 5,000 requests at concurrency 1, three runs each:

run 1 field 5 fields
1 26,202 req/s 26,089 req/s
2 25,874 req/s 24,203 req/s
3 26,080 req/s 26,180 req/s

Within 2% either way. The claim holds: whatever json_set does internally, it isn't re-walking the document for every variable you pull out of it.

What it refuses

json_max_depth defaults to 32. I sent a document nested 40 levels deep and asked for a value at the bottom:

$ curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:18081/ --data-binary @deep40.json
deep=[]

No error, no log line, nothing in error_log. The variable is simply not found, exactly as if the field didn't exist or the JSON were malformed. If you're validating depth-sensitive payloads (deeply nested configuration blobs, arbitrary user-supplied trees), this will silently pass them through as "field missing" rather than flag them as "too deep," and your map block needs to treat those two cases the same way whether you like it or not.

Separately, client_body_early_read is not the boolean it looks like. Its syntax is client_body_early_read _string_ ...;, matched against one or more values, enabled if any is non-empty and isn't "0". Writing client_body_early_read on; works, but only because the literal string "on" happens to be non-empty and not "0" — nginx isn't parsing it as a keyword. client_body_early_read off; would also enable it, which is exactly backward from every other *_module on/off directive in nginx and worth knowing before you copy a pattern from somewhere else in your config.

What I got wrong on the way

My first throughput run reported the new way at roughly 290 times faster than the old way at 50 concurrent clients, and I almost wrote that number down. It turned out to be a harness bug: proxy_pass to the backend defaults to HTTP/1.0 with Connection: close, so without an explicit upstream { keepalive } block, nginx was opening a brand-new TCP connection per request to a backend on loopback, and at concurrency 50 that was exhausting ephemeral ports faster than they could leave TIME_WAIT. The old way wasn't slow because it round-trips to a backend; it was slow because my config made every one of those round trips pay for a fresh handshake. Adding keepalive 64 to the upstream block and proxy_http_version 1.1 dropped the measured gap from 290x to a defensible 13x at low concurrency. The lesson wasn't about JSON parsing at all — it was that an unrealistic proxy config can make the "old way" look artificially bad, which would have flattered the feature I was trying to measure fairly.

Run it yourself 

docker pull nginx:1.31.8

cat > new_way.conf <<'EOF'
worker_processes 1;
events { worker_connections 2048; }
http {
    access_log off;
    client_body_early_read 1;
    upstream backend { server 127.0.0.1:9001; keepalive 64; }
    json_set $event_type $request_body event.type;
    map $event_type $is_invalid_event {
        "payment.created" 0;
        "payment.failed"  0;
        default           1;
    }
    server {
        listen 18091;
        location $is_invalid_event { return 400 "unknown event type\n"; }
        location / {
            proxy_http_version 1.1;
            proxy_set_header Connection "";
            proxy_pass http://backend;
        }
    }
}
EOF

docker run -d --name newway --network host \
  -v "$(pwd)/new_way.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro" nginx:1.31.8

curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:18091/ -d '{"event":{"type":"payment.created"}}'
curl -s -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:18091/ -d '{"event":{"type":"spam.click"}}'

Without a listener on 9001 the valid-case curl just gets a 502, so point something at it first — any script that reads the body and answers 200 will do.

Before you add this, run nginx -V 2>&1 | grep json against whatever you've actually got running. The Ubuntu package doesn't have it. The official Docker image does. If yours does, pull yesterday's access log and count the 400s and 422s your app already wrote. That count is what tells you whether fifteen minutes of config is worth it, not the 13x I got against a toy backend.

articles.title: TC39 `using` Declarations Land in V8 13: What Node.js 24 Developers Get for Free Without TypeScript
articles.description: V8 13 ships TC39's Explicit Resource Management proposal. Node.js 24 developers get deterministic cleanup without TypeScript, `try`/`finally` blocks, or memory leaks.
articles.body_html:
TC39 using Declarations Land in V8 13: What Node.js 24 Developers Get for Free Without TypeScript

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Every JavaScript developer has shipped a file handle that never closed. A database connection that stayed open. A timer that kept the event loop alive.

The pattern is always the same: open a resource, forget to clean it up in one edge case, ship the leak to production. try/finally blocks help, but developers forget them or nest them wrong or skip them when the function returns early.

TC39's Explicit Resource Management proposal gives JavaScript deterministic cleanup. When a using declaration goes out of scope, the runtime calls the resource's disposal method. No try/finally. No manual tracking. No leaks.

V8 13 ships this feature unflagged. Node.js 24 gets it for free. TypeScript developers have been using the syntax since TypeScript 5.2, but the language-level guarantee is newer. Now the runtime enforces it.

Key Takeaways

  • V8 13 ships TC39's using declarations unflagged, available in Node.js 24 without TypeScript or transpilation.
  • Resources declared with using call their Symbol.dispose method when the scope exits, guaranteeing cleanup even on early returns or exceptions.
  • Async resources use await using and Symbol.asyncDispose, making database connections and file handles safe by default.
  • Browser support is arriving in Chrome 131+, Safari 18.2+, and Firefox 135+, with production readiness expected by Q2 2027.
  • The feature eliminates an entire class of resource leaks that try/finally blocks fail to prevent when developers forget to add them.

What TC39's Explicit Resource Management Proposal Actually Does

The TC39 Explicit Resource Management proposal adds two keywords to using and await using. A resource declared with using must implement a Symbol.dispose method. When the block containing the using declaration exits, the runtime calls that method.

// File handle cleanup without manual try/finally
async function processLog(path) {
  using file = await fs.open(path);
  const content = await file.readFile('utf8');
  return parseLogEntries(content);
  // file[Symbol.dispose]() called here automatically
}

The disposal happens at the end of the containing block, not the function. Developers can declare multiple resources with using in the same scope. The runtime disposes them in reverse order, matching the C++ RAII pattern and Rust's drop order.

function transferData(sourcePath, destPath) {
  using source = fs.openSync(sourcePath);
  using dest = fs.openSync(destPath, 'w');

  const buffer = Buffer.allocUnsafe(4096);
  let bytesRead;

  while ((bytesRead = source.readSync(buffer)) > 0) {
    dest.writeSync(buffer, 0, bytesRead);
  }
  // dest disposed first, then source
}

The disposal call happens even when exceptions occur. Developers do not need to wrap using declarations in try/finally. The runtime guarantees the cleanup.

Resources that need asynchronous cleanup implement Symbol.asyncDispose instead. Developers declare them with await using. The runtime awaits the disposal before continuing.

The proposal reached Stage 3 in TC39 in March 2023. V8 shipped the implementation in version 13.0, released October 2024. Node.js 24 (the current LTS as of March 2026) includes V8 13.4.

Using using With File Handles in Node.js 24

Node.js file handles already implement Symbol.dispose and Symbol.asyncDispose. Developers using Node.js 24 can replace try/finally patterns immediately.

File handle lifecycle diagram showing traditional vs using-based cleanup

import { open } from 'node:fs/promises';

// Traditional pattern with manual cleanup
async function readConfigOld(path) {
  let file;
  try {
    file = await open(path);
    const content = await file.readFile('utf8');
    return JSON.parse(content);
  } finally {
    await file?.close();
  }
}

// Using declaration handles cleanup
async function readConfig(path) {
  await using file = await open(path);
  const content = await file.readFile('utf8');
  return JSON.parse(content);
}

The using version removes the try/finally block and the null check. The runtime guarantees the file closes when readConfig returns, whether the function succeeds or throws.

Multiple file operations in the same function become clearer. The traditional pattern requires nested try/finally blocks or a cleanup array. The using declaration handles both cases.

async function mergeConfigs(primaryPath, fallbackPath) {
  await using primary = await open(primaryPath);
  await using fallback = await open(fallbackPath);

  const [primaryData, fallbackData] = await Promise.all([
    primary.readFile('utf8'),
    fallback.readFile('utf8')
  ]);

  return { ...JSON.parse(fallbackData), ...JSON.parse(primaryData) };
  // fallback closed, then primary closed
}

The disposal order matches the declaration order reversed. Developers do not need to track which resources to clean up or in what sequence.

using vs try/finally: Side-by-Side Comparison

The try/finally pattern requires explicit cleanup logic. Developers must remember to add the block, call the right cleanup method, and handle null resources.

The using declaration moves the cleanup guarantee to the language. The runtime handles null checks, disposal calls, and error propagation.

Aspect try/finally using declaration
Cleanup guarantee developer must add finally block runtime enforces cleanup
Null checking manual ?. or if check required runtime handles null/undefined
Multiple resources nested blocks or cleanup array declare multiple using statements
Disposal order developer controls manually reverse declaration order (LIFO)
Error handling must choose to swallow or rethrow disposal errors always propagate
Async cleanup must remember await in finally await using enforces async disposal

Early returns expose the difference. A function with multiple exit points needs cleanup in every path. The try/finally pattern requires a single finally block that covers all returns, or duplicated cleanup logic.

// try/finally requires careful placement
async function processRecord(id) {
  const handle = await db.connect();
  try {
    const record = await handle.query('SELECT * FROM records WHERE id = ?', [id]);
    if (!record) return null; // cleanup happens in finally

    if (record.archived) return null; // cleanup happens in finally

    return transformRecord(record);
  } finally {
    await handle.close();
  }
}

// using declaration works regardless of return path
async function processRecord(id) {
  await using handle = await db.connect();

  const record = await handle.query('SELECT * FROM records WHERE id = ?', [id]);
  if (!record) return null; // handle closed automatically

  if (record.archived) return null; // handle closed automatically

  return transformRecord(record);
}

The using version guarantees cleanup without extra code. Developers add new early returns without updating cleanup logic.

Building Your Own Disposable Resources With Symbol.dispose

Any object with a Symbol.dispose method works with using declarations. The method receives no arguments and returns nothing. The runtime calls it when the scope exits.

class DatabaseTransaction {
  constructor(connection) {
    this.connection = connection;
    this.active = true;
  }

  async commit() {
    if (!this.active) throw new Error('Transaction already finalized');
    await this.connection.commit();
    this.active = false;
  }

  async rollback() {
    if (!this.active) return;
    await this.connection.rollback();
    this.active = false;
  }

  [Symbol.asyncDispose]() {
    return this.rollback();
  }
}

// Automatic rollback on error
async function updateUserBalance(userId, amount) {
  await using tx = new DatabaseTransaction(connection);

  await tx.connection.query(
    'UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + ? WHERE user_id = ?',
    [amount, userId]
  );

  await tx.commit();
  // If commit() throws, rollback() called automatically
  // If we return early, rollback() called automatically
}

The disposal method runs even when the main code throws. Transactions that fail to commit get rolled back. Locks get released. Temporary files get deleted.

Resources that perform synchronous cleanup use Symbol.dispose instead of Symbol.asyncDispose. The runtime calls the method synchronously when the scope exits.

class PerformanceTimer {
  constructor(label) {
    this.label = label;
    this.start = performance.now();
  }

  [Symbol.dispose]() {
    const duration = performance.now() - this.start;
    console.log(`${this.label}: ${duration.toFixed(2)}ms`);
  }
}

function processData(input) {
  using timer = new PerformanceTimer('processData');

  const normalized = normalizeInput(input);
  const validated = validateData(normalized);
  return transformData(validated);
  // Timer logs automatically when function returns
}

A resource can implement both Symbol.dispose and Symbol.asyncDispose. The runtime chooses the async version when the declaration uses await using.

The disposal method should not throw unless the failure represents an unrecoverable error. When disposal throws, the runtime propagates the error. If the main code also threw, the disposal error replaces the original exception.

class FileWriter {
  constructor(path) {
    this.fd = fs.openSync(path, 'w');
    this.closed = false;
  }

  write(data) {
    if (this.closed) throw new Error('Writer closed');
    fs.writeSync(this.fd, data);
  }

  [Symbol.dispose]() {
    if (this.closed) return;
    try {
      fs.closeSync(this.fd);
      this.closed = true;
    } catch (err) {
      console.error('Failed to close file:', err);
      // Don't throw unless close failure is critical
    }
  }
}

The pattern matches how Node.js file handles implement disposal. The Symbol.dispose method calls closeSync() internally. Developers building custom resources should follow the same contract.

Async Disposal With await using and Symbol.asyncDispose

Resources that perform asynchronous cleanup need Symbol.asyncDispose. The method returns a Promise. The runtime awaits the Promise before continuing.

Database connections, network sockets, and file handles all require async disposal. The await using syntax guarantees the cleanup completes before the function returns.

Comparison of sync vs async resource disposal patterns

class DatabaseConnection {
  constructor(config) {
    this.pool = createPool(config);
    this.connection = null;
  }

  async connect() {
    this.connection = await this.pool.getConnection();
    return this;
  }

  async query(sql, params) {
    if (!this.connection) throw new Error('Not connected');
    return this.connection.query(sql, params);
  }

  async [Symbol.asyncDispose]() {
    if (this.connection) {
      await this.connection.release();
      this.connection = null;
    }
  }
}

async function getUserData(userId) {
  await using db = await new DatabaseConnection(config).connect();

  const user = await db.query(
    'SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?',
    [userId]
  );

  const orders = await db.query(
    'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = ?',
    [userId]
  );

  return { user, orders };
  // Connection released automatically
}

The await using declaration ensures the connection returns to the pool. Developers do not need to track whether the function succeeded or failed.

Multiple async resources dispose in reverse order. The runtime awaits each disposal before starting the next.

async function syncData(sourcePath, destPath) {
  await using source = await fetch(sourcePath).then(r => r.body);
  await using dest = await fs.open(destPath, 'w');

  for await (const chunk of source) {
    await dest.write(chunk);
  }
  // dest closed first, then source closed
}

The disposal order prevents race conditions. A destination file closes before the source stream, ensuring all data writes complete.

Mixing sync and async disposal in the same scope works. The runtime calls sync disposal methods immediately and awaits async disposal methods.

async function processWithMetrics(dataPath) {
  using timer = new PerformanceTimer('process'); // sync disposal
  await using file = await open(dataPath); // async disposal

  const content = await file.readFile('utf8');
  return parseData(content);
  // file closed (awaited), then timer logged (sync)
}

The runtime disposes resources in reverse declaration order regardless of disposal type. Async disposal awaits completion before moving to the next resource.

For more patterns on resource management and cleanup strategies, see 10 JavaScript and Node.js Tips That Knock Away Multiple Concepts and 5 Node.js Tricks to Make JavaScript Development Fascinating.

Browser Support, Runtime Availability, and When You Can Ship This

V8 13 shipped using declarations unflagged in October 2024. Chrome 131 (stable November 2024) includes the feature. Safari 18.2 (shipped December 2024) supports it. Firefox 135 (planned February 2025) will include it.

Node.js 24 (LTS since March 2026) includes V8 13.4. Developers targeting Node.js 24 can use using declarations without transpilation. Deno 2.1 (shipped January 2025) supports the feature. Bun 1.2 (shipped December 2024) implements it.

Runtime Version V8 version using support
Node.js 24 LTS 24.0.0+ 13.4 Yes (unflagged)
Node.js 22 LTS 22.0.0+ 12.4 No
Deno 2.1.0+ 13.2 Yes (unflagged)
Bun 1.2.0+ - Yes (native)
Chrome 131.0+ 13.1 Yes (unflagged)
Safari 18.2+ - Yes (native)
Firefox 135.0+ - Planned Q1 2025

Browser support lags server runtimes. Developers shipping client-side code should check caniuse.com for current browser coverage. Transpilers like Babel support the syntax through the @babel/plugin-proposal-explicit-resource-management plugin.

TypeScript 5.2 added support for using declarations in August 2023. Developers using TypeScript get type checking for Symbol.dispose and Symbol.asyncDispose methods. The compiler emits JavaScript that calls disposal methods in finally blocks when targeting environments without native support.

The Node.js collaboration summit in April 2025 discussed integrating AsyncContext with resource management. The TC39 Disposable AsyncContext proposal combines using syntax with AsyncLocalStorage. That feature remains in Stage 1.

Production readiness depends on the target environment. Node.js 24 projects can adopt using declarations immediately. Browser-based projects should wait until Firefox 135 reaches stable (expected Q1 2025) or use transpilation. By Q2 2027, all major browsers and runtimes will support the feature natively.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I use using with objects that don't implement Symbol.dispose?

No. The runtime throws a TypeError if a using declaration receives an object without a Symbol.dispose method (or Symbol.asyncDispose for await using). Wrap non-disposable resources in an object that implements the disposal interface.

What happens if Symbol.dispose throws an error?

The disposal error propagates to the caller. If the main code also threw, the disposal error replaces the original exception. Write disposal methods that catch and log errors instead of throwing unless the failure is unrecoverable.

Does using work in loops and conditional blocks?

Yes. A using declaration inside a loop or conditional block disposes the resource when the block exits, not when the function returns. Resources declared in a loop body dispose on each iteration.

Can I manually dispose a resource declared with using?

Yes. Call the Symbol.dispose method directly. The runtime skips the automatic disposal if the method already ran. Most disposable resources track their state and become no-ops after the first disposal call.

How does this compare to Go's defer or Rust's Drop?

JavaScript's using provides deterministic cleanup like Rust's Drop trait. The disposal happens at the end of the block, not the function. Go's defer runs cleanup when the function returns, which differs from the block-scoped behavior. The reverse-order disposal matches both languages.

Why This Matters More Than TypeScript's using Keyword

TypeScript 5.2 shipped using declarations 14 months before V8. TypeScript developers have been writing the syntax since August 2023. The language-level support changes the guarantee.

TypeScript compiles using declarations to try/finally blocks when targeting runtimes without native support. The cleanup happens, but the TypeScript compiler generates the code. Developers targeting older runtimes still ship transpiled JavaScript.

V8's native implementation moves the cleanup guarantee to the runtime. The disposal call happens regardless of transpilation. Developers targeting Node.js 24 skip the build step entirely. No TypeScript compiler. No Babel plugin. The runtime enforces cleanup.

The feature eliminates a class of bugs that try/finally blocks fail to prevent. Developers forget to add cleanup code. They nest blocks wrong. They return early without cleanup. The using declaration removes those failure modes.

Database connections stay open. File handles leak. Network sockets time out. These failures happen in production because cleanup logic lives in application code. The runtime guarantee moves cleanup from developer discipline to language semantics.

Node.js 24 makes this guarantee available without TypeScript. Developers running plain JavaScript get deterministic cleanup. The runtime handles disposal. The feature works in scripts, REPL sessions, and production code. For more on leveraging modern Node.js features, see Convenient Tactics of Logging in Node.js and JavaScript in the Browser.

Every resource leak that ships to production represents a try/finally block developers forgot to write. The using declaration removes that decision. Cleanup happens automatically. The runtime guarantees it.

Sources

  • V8 | Node.js v26.13.1 Documentation

articles.title: remove.bg Dies Dec 1 — I Ran the Same 3 Photos Through the Free Replacements and Timed Them
articles.description: December 1, 2026, 9:00 AM CET. That's when remove.bg's standalone site goes dark for good.  If you've...
articles.body_html:
December 1, 2026, 9:00 AM CET. That's when remove.bg's standalone site goes dark for good.

If you've ever dragged a product photo onto that site, you know the deal: free, fast, and the catch was always the resolution. The free tier only ever gave you preview-sized downloads, up to 0.25 megapixels, per remove.bg's own help page. Anything bigger cost credits, about $9 a month for 40 images. After December 1, background removal moves into Canva — on the paid tier — and people using the remove.bg service directly are pointed at Leonardo.ai instead.

So the question isn't whether to switch. It's what to switch to. I spent this morning running the same three photos through the free option I could actually measure: rembg, the open-source tool that runs on your own machine — and timed every step. No uploads, no credits, no account. Here's what it really costs.

The three photos

I picked three photos that cover the jobs people actually use background removal for:

  • A product shot: a red Nike shoe on a plain background, 1200×800
  • A portrait: a woman in a denim jacket and hoodie, 1200×1800
  • A landscape: a mountain lake at dusk, 1200×801, no obvious subject

The shoe and the portrait are the fair test. The landscape is the trap. I'll come back to it, because what happened there matters more than the clean wins.

What I ran

rembg 2.0.87, the standard u2net model, on an ordinary machine: 4 CPUs, 8 GB of RAM, Ubuntu 24.04. Nothing fancy, no graphics card. The install is one line:

pip install "rembg[cpu]"

The quotes matter: plain rembg installs without the engine it needs to run, and the first thing you'll see is an error telling you to install it with CPU support. I found that out the slow way.

First run downloads the model: 176 MB, about 17 seconds on my connection, 27 seconds total before the first photo started processing. After that, the model sits on your disk and every run after is just the processing time.

The numbers

Photo Size Time Output Transparent
Shoe (product) 1200×800 8.2s 1200×800 PNG, 632 KB 73.5%
Portrait 1200×1800 8.4s 1200×1800 PNG, 1.56 MB 66.8%
Landscape 1200×801 6.8s 1200×801 PNG, 100 KB 71.7%

Two things jump out. First, full resolution is kept. Every output came back at exactly the input dimensions, which is the whole point. remove.bg's free tier would have handed me back a 0.25-megapixel version of that portrait. Second, the times are all in the same band: 7–8 seconds a photo on a plain CPU. Not instant, not painful. A batch of 40 product shots is about five minutes of waiting.

What the cut-outs actually look like

Numbers don't tell you whether the edges are any good, so I looked at all three.

The shoe is the clean win. The outline follows the knit texture, the laces stay intact, the Nike logo on the tongue is untouched. If you sell things online, this is the result you need, and it cost nothing.

The portrait is nearly as good. The glasses survive, the hoodie strings survive, and the hair, usually where these tools fall apart, holds up along the edges. There's a faint softness where the hair meets the background if you zoom right in, but at normal viewing size you'd never spot it.

The landscape is the honest failure, and it's the most useful result of the three. A cut-out tool needs a subject. A mountain lake doesn't have one. The tool kept a smudge of sky in the middle and threw away the mountains, the water, everything that made it a photo. The "71.7% transparent" figure looks fine in a table and means nothing — the remaining 28% is a grey blob. If your photo has no clear subject, no background remover will save it, free or paid.

The costs nobody puts in the headline

Free doesn't mean zero cost. Here's the real bill for the local route:

  • 176 MB, once. The model downloads the first time and stays. On a slow connection that's a coffee break, not a dealbreaker.
  • About 8 seconds a photo on a plain CPU. A graphics card would cut that, but most laptops don't have one to spare.
  • PNG files get big. The shoe came in as a 128 KB JPEG and went out as a 632 KB PNG. Transparency costs bytes. If you're putting cut-outs on a website, compress them afterwards. The same tool will happily eat its own output.
  • You do the organising. No website, no history, no "your recent images" page. Your files live where you put them.

Against that, the bill for staying with the old way after December 1 is a subscription: Canva's paid tier for the background tool, or credits somewhere else. For occasional use, the local route wins on price by a distance. For someone cutting out fifty product shots a week inside a team that already lives in Canva, the subscription might still be the saner choice. That's a question about how you work, not about quality.

Two options I didn't time

Fairness check: rembg wasn't the only free name on the list, and I didn't run the other two myself.

APIC Web is a free editor built by a 13-year-old developer, and it runs the same kind of cut-out entirely in your own browser. Photos never leave your device. Its own write-up is blunt about the limits: exporting needs a Google sign-in, the first run is slow because the model downloads, and there's a banner ad. It also has a batch mode that would handle those fifty product shots in one go. I didn't put it through the same timed run, so I won't quote speeds for it — but on paper it's the closest thing to a drop-in replacement for the remove.bg website, and the privacy story is stronger, since nothing uploads at all.

Canva's free plan doesn't include the background remover; plan summaries list it as a paid feature. That's the trade waiting on December 1: the tool you used for free becomes part of a subscription. If you already pay for Canva, nothing changes for you. If you don't, that's the moment to look elsewhere.

What I'd actually do

If you cut out backgrounds a few times a month: product shots, profile photos, a thumbnail here and there — install rembg today and forget about December 1. One install, one 176 MB download, and the tool is yours forever. It handles the two jobs that matter, product and portrait, at full resolution, for nothing.

If you do it in bulk, look at APIC's batch mode as well. Same idea, in a browser tab, no install.

And if your photo has no clear subject, save yourself the trouble. No tool in this list will invent one for you.

Sources

  • remove.bg shutdown date and free-tier limit (0.25 MP): remove.bg's own help page, via APIC vs Canva, Adobe Express, Photopea & remove.bg (Nov 8, 2026) and remove.bg Is Shutting Down — Here's a Free, No-Upload Alternative (Nov 13, 2026)
  • APIC details (free, no credits, sign-in to export, batch mode): the author's own write-up, same link above
  • Canva Background Remover on paid plans: third-party plan summaries, cited in the same write-up — check Canva's pricing page for the current picture
  • All timings, file sizes and quality notes: my own runs this morning, evidence in runs/removebg-alternatives/ (photos, outputs, timing log)

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: Bye, live regions. Hello, ariaNotify()
articles.description: In September 2026, ariaNotify() was introduced as a new web API method to replace live regions. We...
articles.body_html:
In September 2026, ariaNotify() was introduced as a new web API method to replace live regions. We are going to learn when we have to use it, which compliance criteria it meets and its benefits.

Hello, ariaNotify() method!! The title might be a clickbait, because we are far from replacing live regions, buuut... I am super excited about this new feature. I have been waiting for it since 2024 when it was announced in the WAI-ARIA 1.3 draft and it finally becomes baseline, in September of this year (2026) having complete support on Chrome, Firefox, Edge and Safari. So, you might be wondering why the hype, let's find out.

What is ariaNotify()? It is a web API's method that was presented as a programmatic way to trigger screen reader announcements. Yes, same thing as live regions, but the main difference is that live regions are attached to a DOM element and to achieve this now we have to inject hidden text into a DOM element where the change lives, therefore it only announces a text when there is a structural modification on the content. On the contrary, ariaNotify() queues the text to be announced by screen readers using JavaScript.

Markup of Live Regions

A summary of how live regions works nowadays. They need a combination of HTML + CSS + JavaScript to work properly.

<!-- an empty DOM element -->
<p role="status"></p>

// Then, injects the upate on the empty DOM element
const region = document.querySelector('[role="status"]')
region.textContent = '3 results'

Roles

  • role="status": it is used for text that are advisory and not important enough to interrupt. It implies aria-live="polite" and aria-atomic="true".
  • role="alert": it is used for important and/or time-sensitive text and it interrupts what the screen reader is currently saying. It implies aria-live="assertive" and aria-atomic="true".
  • role="log": it is used for new entries in order, like a chat or live updates. It implies aria-live="polite".

WAI-ARIA

  • aria-live: it has three values, polite which waits until the user is idle, assertive which interrupts what the user is perceiving, off which indicates that the changes on a region will only be announced when the user focuses on it.
  • aria-atomic: its value can be true which means that the whole region will be announced when any part of it changes, or false which means that only the part of the region that changes is announced, for example, a clock going from 17.33 to 17.34, only the “34” will be announced.
  • aria-busy: it is used on live regions that might be modified to let the user know when they have been modified. Its value can be true which tells the screen reader that it may wait until the changes are finished before announcing them, or false which means that nothing happens and nothing will be announced until the task is finished.
  • aria-relevant: it is an optional attribute of live regions and it is just a suggestion to assistive technologies. Its values can be additions which refers to element nodes that are added to the accessibility tree within the live region, all, which it is a shorthand for additions removals text, removals which refers to any text content within the live region that is removed from the accessibility tree, or text which refers to text content or a text alternative that is added to any descendant in the accessibility tree of the live region.

Markup of ariaNotify() 


element.ariaNotify('Draft saved.', { priority: 'high' })
  1. Host element or document It is the element that will contain the announcement. It could be the Element in the accessibility tree, or the Document.
  2. Method ariaNotify() The method itself. It is called on the host and it contains the announcement and the options.
  3. Announcement 'Draft saved.' Required. It is the announcement text. Without it there is a TypeError.
  4. Options { priority: 'high' } Optional. If it is omitted or a value that is not on the dictionary is being placed, the value by default would be ‘normal’.
  5. Priority priority: 'high' | 'normal' normal, the default, is spoken after what is being spoken; high interrupts it.

Parallels with Live Regions

In Live Region In ariaNotify Parallelism
role="status", aria-live="polite" { priority: 'normal' } (the default) Both are polite regions and wait until the previous announcement has finished before announcing.
role="alert", aria-live="assertive" { priority: 'high' } Both interrupt what is being spoken to announce the latest message.
element.textContent = 'Draft saved.' element.ariaNotify('Draft saved.') The message to be announced.
aria-atomic="true" announcement text aria-atomic makes a whole region announceable when any part of it changes. In live regions it is applicable to the hidden string to announce but in ariaNotify the announcement text is already the argument to announce

Live Region 

<p role="status" aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true"></p>

<p role="alert" aria-atomic="true"></p>

const polite = document.querySelector('[role="status"]')
const assertive = document.querySelector('[role="alert"]')

polite.textContent = 'Draft saved.'
assertive.textContent = 'Could not save the draft.'

ariaNotify() 

<button type="button" lang="en">Save draft</button>

const element = document.querySelector('button')

element.ariaNotify('Draft saved.')
element.ariaNotify('Could not save the draft.', {
  priority: 'high',
})

In my opinion, the ariaNotify arrived to simplify the knowledge around announcements. In the past, having to communicate the knowledge about live regions was the biggest challenge for accessibility experts so having a method that with a single line of code covered the screen reader announcements without without hardcoding hidden text is refreshing.

Live Regions vs ariaNotify(): Use Cases

In this section, we will learn with use case examples how ariaNotify() simplifies the work and meets the WCAG success criterion to be compliant.

Here you can test the examples

Should I Document or Should I Element?

Neither of the MDN page for ariaNotify() in Document nor the MDN page for ariaNotify() in Element make a clear distinction between whether to attach the ariaNotify method to the Document or to the Element, but we can state that the choice is about the message per se. Based on that, I created the following table to help decide where to attach the method based on semantics and context.

Another thing worth mentioning is that the language of the announcement by default is, it comes from the lang attribute on the html element. If you want a dedicated section of the page to have a different language, set it explicitly.

Situation Where Why
Announcement about connection, a new version, session update, and a total upate Document The announcement is not tied to an action by the user or to an update in a region, but to a global update that improves or modifies the experience.
Announcement about a thing happening in a section of the page. It could be a count, a total updated, a progress bar, etc Element The announcement has a context, a scope
Announcement of something that has been removed from the DOM Document The Element does no longer exists in the DOM, so the announcement should be made from the Document

Reusable and Global Solution for Announcements Using Just ariaNotify()

In my lib of methods, last month I implemented a reusable function to dispatch announcements programmatically using the ariaNotify() method.

  1. A function to check if the native HTML element supports ariaNotify() 
   export const hasAriaNotify = () =>
     typeof Element !== 'undefined' && 'ariaNotify' in Element.prototype
  1. Create a type (if you are using TypeScript) to tell TypeScript the method may exist and what it takes. 
   type Notifier = {
      ariaNotify?: (announcement: string, options?: { priority: Priority }) => void
    }
  1. Then we have to create a notify function 
   export function notify(
      from: Element | Document,
      message: string,
      priority: Priority = 'normal',
    ) {
      const native = hasAriaNotify()
      const send = () => {
        (from as unknown as Notifier).ariaNotify?.(message, { priority })
      }
      if (native) return send()
    }
  • The function has 3 mandatory parameters: from which checks if the method is being attached to an Element or Document, message which is the string of texts to be announced and priority which is the type of announcement that the screen reader should do.
  • If native is true, we are going to attach the method to the Element/Document and dispatch the action.
    1. The reusable function can be used in the following way: 
   notify(bar, 'report.pdf uploaded.')

Screen Readers

Click here to discover how screen readers announce the announcements of ariaNotify method

WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion - Level AA

Success Criterion Explanation
4.1.3 Status Messages (AA) as in Technique ARIA27, the progress should be announced.
3.3.1 Error Identification (A) For example, a failed upload should be announced with high priority

Browser Support

According to MDN, this is the list of browsers that support ariaNotify on their latest update since September 2026. Oldest versions might not support ariaNotify.

  • Chrome version 141
  • Edge version 141
  • Firefox version 150
  • Opera version 125
  • Safari version 27
  • Chrome Android version 141
  • Firefox Android version 150
  • Opera Android version 93
  • Safari on iOS version 27
  • Samsung Browser version 30
  • WebView Android version 141
  • WebView on iOS version 27

Resources

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/ariaNotify
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/ariaNotify
  • https://w3c.github.io/aria/#ARIANotifyMixin

articles.body_html:
Sometimes, in my spare time, I google my own domain.

saturumah.net — that's mine. I just wanted to see what Google result about it.

What surprised me was the top result: ossuary.saturumah.net. That is not what I expected. I had set up some Search Console experiments, but I had not yet registered link to google search console...oh yes, thats nice :)

Oh well. Whatever. Let me try Gemini for that — typing into the AI capability in the browser.

The responses were genuinely impressive. Gemini understood the code better than I did. It understood the Sentry integration, the GridFS storage layer, the TigerData hypertable — the whole architecture.

What made the conversation interesting was how I engaged with it. I tapped the suggested follow-up questions again and again. Ask, answer, tap, repeat. By the end, I had a full technical deep-dive.

I want to share the story with you here. I hope this post can hang on your dev.to homepage for a bit. 🕯️

Here is the JSONL:

OSSUARY: The Last Packet claude-sonnet-4-20250514
You

"OSSUARY: The Last Packet"

Agent

OSSUARY: The Last Packet is an open-source project and digital séance tool created for the Hacktoberfest AI Challenge ("Ghost in the Machine").What It Does
- Digital Séance for Dead Domains: You type or "whisper" a defunct or dead website domain into the interface.
- Archivist, Not Inventor: Instead of letting an AI hallucinate fake horror stories, the tool reconstructs the "ghost" of the domain using real archived data—pulling from the last network packet the server sent, the final snapshot from the Wayback Machine, and the last written trace before shutdown.
- Output: It generates a first-person narrative and audio response voiced by an AI, preserving the digital footprint as an archived memorial rather than cheap fiction.
You can read the full technical write-up on DEV Community.Would you like to explore how the technical data pipeline works or see details on the open-weight models used to build it?

You

how the technical data pipeline works

Agent

The technical data pipeline for OSSUARY: The Last Packet operates as a five-stage architecture designed to verify a domain's death before generating any AI response. The frontend runs on Vercel (React 19, Vite 8) and sends requests to a persistent Express backend hosted on Render to avoid serverless timeout limits.1. Parallel Reconnaissance (/api/recon)When a user enters a domain, the backend runs four external checks in parallel with strict timeouts:

  • DNS Lookup. Checks active A and AAAA records via dns.promises.resolve.
  • WHOIS Registration. Queries domain registration status using a three-layer fallback chain (IP2WHOIS, RDAP, and WhoisXMLAPI).
  • Wayback Machine CDX. Queries the Internet Archive to pull both the earliest snapshot (used as the "born" date) and the last pre-death snapshot.
