articles.title: The Code I Wrote and No Longer Understand
articles.description: I wrote this file, and I cannot read it.  That is the whole confession. There is no twist coming. The...
articles.body_html:
I wrote this file, and I cannot read it.

That is the whole confession. There is no twist coming. The file is called billing_reconcile.py. It is 214 lines long, and every one of those lines was typed by me, eight months ago, in a week I barely remember. I opened it on a Tuesday morning because a customer had been charged twice for the same order. $63.20, twice. Someone had to find out why. That someone was me. I stared at the first function for eleven minutes. I know it was eleven minutes because I checked the clock twice, the way you check the clock in a waiting room.

The function was called normalize_line_items. I remembered writing the name. I remembered feeling good about the name, the way you feel good about naming a dog. What I did not remember was what it did. It took a list in, gave a list back, and in between it did something with a dictionary, a date, and a variable called temp2. There was a temp2. Which means there was a temp1 somewhere, and I could not find it, and I did not want to know what temp1 had done to earn its number.

My own comments were the worst part. I had left comments. I am the kind of person who leaves comments, and I say that the way people say they floss: proudly, and not entirely truthfully. Above the trickiest block there was a comment that said: "# don't touch this, it works." That was all. No explanation of what "this" was. No explanation of what "works" meant. Just a warning from a stranger who happened to have my name on the commit.

Another one said: "# TODO: fix later (it is later)." I had written that. I had written a joke to myself, eight months ago, and then forgotten the joke and the fix. Past me thought he was funny. Past me was also, apparently, in a hurry.

I should explain the hurry, because the hurry is the whole story, and it is also the excuse I have been rehearsing in case anyone asks.

Eight months ago, we had a deadline. A client was going live on Friday, and the billing page had to stop double-charging people by Thursday, and the fix landed on me on Wednesday afternoon, because I was the only one who had touched that part of the code before. I was. I had touched it. Once. Six months before that. I said yes anyway, because "yes" is the easiest word in the world when someone is standing at your desk.

I wrote the file on Wednesday night, starting at about nine, finishing at about twenty past midnight. I remember the shape of the night better than the code: the music too loud, the coffee gone cold twice, the feeling of going fast. Fast is a drug when you are behind. Every line worked on the first try, or the second, and I did not stop to ask why. I named a variable temp2 because temp1 was taken and I was in no mood to negotiate with myself. I wrote "# don't touch this, it works" at 12:07 a.m., and I meant it as a note to future me, and future me read it eight months later and understood none of it.

The demo went fine. The client went live. The file sat there, working, like a locked room in my own house. I never opened it again. Why would I? It worked. That was the deal I had made with it: it works, I don't touch it. Eight months of peace, bought with one comment.

Then Tuesday morning, the double charge. $63.20, twice. And there I was, standing outside the locked room, holding a key I had made myself, unable to remember which way it turned.

I did what anyone does in that position. I lied, a little, and bought time. I told the team I was going to clean the file up before I fixed it. "Refactor" was the word I used. Refactor is a wonderful word. It sounds like work. It sounds like improvement. It sounds like a man who understands the thing he is about to improve. What I actually did was sit down and re-learn my own code from scratch, the way you would re-learn a language you spoke as a child, one line at a time, with a notebook open beside me.

I started at the top and worked down, writing what each block did in plain words, like a translation. "This part takes the messy list from the payment page." "This part checks the dates." "This part, I think, throws away the duplicates." By noon I had three pages of notebook and a headache. By two o'clock I had found the bug. It was in the part I had marked "don't touch." Of course it was. The duplicate check compared the wrong two things, and it had been comparing the wrong two things for eight months, and the only reason nobody had noticed was that the wrong two things were usually the same. Usually. Not always. Not on Tuesday.

I fixed it in four lines. Four lines, after five hours of reading. I sat there for a while after the fix, looking at the notebook. Five hours of reading, four lines of fix. I decided to think about something else.

The dread, though, was not the bug. The dread was standup the next morning. I could already hear it: "Salam, can you walk us through the billing fix?" And I would have to stand there and walk six people through a file I had only just learned to read, and someone would ask why temp2 was called temp2, and I would have to say "because I was in a hurry at midnight" in front of everyone. I spent the evening drafting my answer in my head, the way you draft a text you never send, and every version sounded worse than the last.

Priya found me at my desk the next morning, still staring at the notebook. Priya sits two desks over. She has been doing this longer than me, and she has the calm of a person who has seen worse. She looked at my notebook — three pages of translation, boxes, arrows, one frustrated doodle of a locked door — and she said, "Yours too?"

"Yours too?" I said.

She told me about her file. It is called email_digests.py. She wrote it a year ago, in a week she describes as "a blur with a deadline in it." She opened it last month and could not follow it. Her comment, the one she remembers, says: "# I don't know why this works and I am afraid to find out." She said it the way you admit you still sleep with the light on sometimes. Not proud. Not ashamed either. Just true.

We sat there for a while, two people who had written code they could no longer read, with coffee going cold on both our desks. Then she said, "I started leaving notes. At the top of every file. For future me. Like a letter." She showed me one, on her phone. It said: "Dear future me, this file sends the weekly email. The weird part in the middle is because Tuesdays are special. Sorry about Tuesdays. — past me."

That evening, I went back to my file and wrote one. At the top, above everything, in plain words:

"Dear future me, this file takes the messy list from the payment page and makes it tidy. The dictionary is the price list. temp2 is the discount. Sorry about temp2. — past me"

I saved the file. Two hundred and fourteen lines, and now the first four were a letter. The stranger and I were on speaking terms again.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: Bus factor 1 is the default: per-language ownership in 195 popular repos
articles.description: Bus factor is the fewest people who made 80% of a file's commits. In the median popular repo, 60% of files have a bus factor of 1. Compute yours from git.
articles.body_html:
TL;DR

  • Bus factor is the fewest people who together made 80% of a file's commits; a bus factor of 1 means one person made 80% or more of them.
  • In the median of 195 popular open-source repos (1,000+ GitHub stars), 60% of production files have a bus factor of 1, and in 124 of the 195 those files are the majority.
  • Busy files are more shared: in the median repo, 25% of hotspot files have a bus factor of 1.
  • Numbers come from repowise's index of those 195 repos (November 2026), plus a git shortlog script run on a full clone of Django.

Bus factor (also called truck factor) is the number of people who would have to disappear before nobody left understands a piece of code. A bus factor of 1 means one person holds it.

It sounds like a warning sign. Across 195 popular open-source repositories, it is the normal state of most files.

How do you calculate bus factor?

For a single file: the fewest authors who together made 80% of its commits. If one person made 80% or more of the commits, the file has a bus factor of 1. If it takes two people to reach 80%, it is 2, and so on.

Commits are a rough proxy for knowledge, but every repo already has them. git blame is worse for this, because a formatter run or a big rename hands whole files to whoever pressed the button.

Compute it for one file

git shortlog -sn counts commits per author and sorts them, highest first. Walk down that list until you pass 80%:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# busfactor.sh <file> [git log options]
f="$1"; shift
git shortlog -sn --no-merges "$@" HEAD -- "$f" |
  awk '{c[NR] = $1; t += $1}
       END {for (i = 1; i <= NR; i++) {s += c[i]; if (s >= 0.8 * t) {print i; exit}}}'

On a full clone of Django (HEAD 6a8248f, 10 November 2026), for the QuerySet module:

$ ./busfactor.sh django/db/models/query.py
54
$ ./busfactor.sh django/db/models/query.py --since="2 years ago"
20

Fifty-four people made 80% of the commits to query.py over 21 years, and 20 people over the last two. That is about as far from 1 as a file gets.

Two details matter in that script. HEAD is explicit because git shortlog with no revision reads standard input when it is not attached to a terminal, which inside a script means it prints nothing. And the --since option is not decoration. The people who wrote a file in 2012 are not necessarily the people who could fix it today, so the window you pick changes the answer.

Run it over every .py file under django/:

git ls-files 'django/*.py' | while read -r f; do
  echo "$(./busfactor.sh "$f") $f"
done | awk '$1 == 1 {b++} END {print b " of " NR " files have bus factor 1"}'

151 of 909 files have bus factor 1

Now the same loop with --since="2 years ago" passed through, counting only the files that had commits in that window:

git ls-files 'django/*.py' | while read -r f; do
  echo "$(./busfactor.sh "$f" --since="2 years ago") $f"
done | awk 'NF == 2 {n++; if ($1 == 1) b++} END {print b " of " n " files with commits have bus factor 1"}'

136 of 460 files with commits have bus factor 1

17% over Django's whole history, 30% over the last two years. Same code, same rule, a different window. Django is also one of the most widely shared codebases in open source. Most projects look different.

How common is a bus factor of 1 in open source?

I looked at production source files (tests, generated and vendored code excluded) in 195 public repositories with 1,000+ GitHub stars each, using the same 80% rule on each repo's indexed git history.

  • In the median repo, 60% of production files have a bus factor of 1.
  • In 124 of the 195 repos (64%), files with a bus factor of 1 are the majority.

By primary language (GitHub's label for the repo), median share of production files with a bus factor of 1:

Language Repos Files with bus factor 1
Rust 15 79%
TypeScript 52 70%
C# 10 66% (small group, indicative)
Python 51 57%
Go 22 49%
JavaScript 13 45% (small group, indicative)
C++ 8 44% (small group, indicative)
All 195 195 60%

I would not read too much into the language order. Bus factor depends heavily on how long a project has existed and how many regular contributors it has, and those vary more between repos than between languages. A three-year-old project has had far less time to spread knowledge around than Django has in 21.

Are the most-changed files single-owner?

The more useful number is about hotspots, the files that change most often. If the busiest files were also single-owner, that would be a real risk: lots of change going through one person's head.

The data says the opposite. In the median repo, 25% of hotspot files have a bus factor of 1, against 60% of all production files. Pooled across the 195 repos, 34% of 20,941 hotspot files are single-owner. Code that changes a lot tends to get touched by more people, which is what you would hope.

So a bus factor of 1 on a file nobody edits is mostly fine. The case worth acting on is a file that is still changing often while its main author has gone quiet.

What should you do about a bus factor of 1?

  • Find the overlap first: files with a bus factor of 1 that are also in the top 10% by recent churn (lines added plus deleted in the last 90 days, which git log --numstat gives you). Start with that list.
  • Route reviews on those files to a second person on purpose, even when the owner could review alone.
  • Ask the owner for a short note on intent: why it is shaped like this, what not to change. Ten lines in a docstring or an ADR outlast a handover meeting.
  • Do not chase a number. A bus factor of 2 on a stable utility file is not worth a reorg.

The full method, including .mailmap for people with several email addresses and how to run this across a whole repo, is in this guide on measuring bus factor from git. For a large repo you can browse, Grafana's owners page shows bus factor per file across its 10,000+ production files. At its last index, 24% of them had a bus factor of 1, well under the median.

How does your team handle single-owner files that still change every week?

How I got these numbers

The cohort is 195 of the most-starred public repositories indexed on repowise (1,000+ GitHub stars each, 253,688 production source files, November 2026), each measured at its own latest index between May and November 2026. The cohort-wide ownership numbers are finding 8 of the code health 2026 report. Bus factor is computed per production file from each repo's indexed git history with the 80% rule above. No author names were collected or used. The Django runs are the script above on a full clone at 6a8248f.

FAQ

What does the term bus factor mean?
Bus factor, also called truck factor, is the number of people who would have to leave a project before nobody left understands a piece of code. Here it is measured per file as the fewest authors who together made 80% of its commits.

How do you calculate bus factor from git?
Run git shortlog -sn --no-merges HEAD -- <file> to count commits per author, highest first, then add authors down the list until you pass 80% of the commits. The number of authors you needed is the bus factor. Add --since to measure only recent history.

Is a bus factor of 1 bad?
Not on its own. It is the normal state of 60% of production files in the median popular repo, and a single-owner file nobody edits is mostly fine. The case to act on is a file that still changes often while its main author has gone quiet.

articles.title: OpenAI timeout=60 Never Fired on a Stream With Keep-Alives
articles.description: The openai Python SDK's timeout=60 limits each socket read, not the request, so a streamed completion...
articles.body_html:
The openai Python SDK's timeout=60 limits each socket read, not the request, so a streamed completion that receives an SSE keep-alive comment every 15 seconds never times out, even though your loop never sees an event. Put a wall clock around the whole attempt instead: with AsyncOpenAI, asyncio.timeout(30) ended the same stalled stream at 30.0 to 30.1 seconds in every run.

This story was written with the assistance of an AI writing program. The numbers come from openai 2.43.0 and httpx 0.28.1 on Python 3.14.4, run against a local fake OpenAI-compatible endpoint over plain HTTP and TLS. I did not test OpenAI's own API, and I do not know whether it sends comment lines.

The Server Sends One Token, Then Only Heartbeats

The fake endpoint answers POST /v1/chat/completions with text/event-stream, sends one normal data: chunk containing "Hello", and then stops producing tokens. In the silent variant it sends nothing more and holds the connection open. In the heartbeat variant it writes : keep-alive every 15 seconds and never sends [DONE].

The client copies the settings of a real pipeline I reviewed this week: OpenAI(timeout=60.0, max_retries=0), stream=True, and a for chunk in stream loop. Each scenario ran as its own process under a 150-second timeout command, so exit code 124 means it was still blocked when the cap hit.

Silence Times Out at 60 Seconds; Heartbeats Never Do

Result lines from one plain-HTTP run, all scenarios in parallel:

{"result": "exception", "type": "httpx.ReadTimeout", "msg": "timed out", "is_openai_APITimeoutError": false, "t": 60.6, "scenario": "silent", "tls": false}
{"scenario": "comments", "exit": 124}
{"result": "exception", "type": "builtins.TimeoutError", "msg": "", "t": 30.1, "scenario": "comments-async", "tls": false}

The silent stream failed at 60.4 to 60.6 seconds across three runs, as expected. The heartbeat stream was still waiting at 150 seconds in all three, including the TLS run. Nothing in the loop body ran after the first chunk.

Look at the type in the silent case: httpx.ReadTimeout, not openai.APITimeoutError. The SDK converts timeouts into its own exception while it sends the request; once you are iterating, the raw httpx exception comes through. An except openai.APITimeoutError around a stream misses it.

Why the Loop Sees Nothing but the Timer Resets

Two pieces combine. First, the SDK's SSE decoder discards comment lines: openai/_streaming.py has if line.startswith(":"): return None, which is correct for the format, so your code never learns that bytes arrived. Second, timeout=60 becomes httpx.Timeout(60), which sets the same 60 seconds for connect, read, write and pool acquisition. None of the four is a total. The read limit restarts on every successful read, and each comment is one.

So the 60 seconds measure silence on the socket, not progress on your completion. A heartbeat every 15 seconds means the socket is never silent for 60.

I hit the same shape with requests last week, when a server dripping one byte every three seconds kept timeout=5 busy for 57 seconds. The difference here is that the bytes are invisible: no partial content, no log line, nothing that tells you the call is still alive.

Who Actually Sends Comment Lines

This is not exotic. The HTML Standard's section on server-sent events suggests sending a comment line every 15 seconds or so, because some legacy proxies drop connections that go quiet. OpenRouter's streaming docs say it occasionally sends comments such as : OPENROUTER PROCESSING to prevent connection timeouts. Any gateway, proxy or self-hosted server that follows that advice turns a per-read timeout into no timeout while the model is stuck.

A Wall-Clock Budget Ended It at 30 Seconds

With AsyncOpenAI, I put asyncio.timeout around the request and the iteration together. This is the exact function I ran this morning, pointed at the fake endpoint through OPENAI_BASE_URL:

import asyncio
import openai
client = openai.AsyncOpenAI(timeout=60.0, max_retries=0)
async def ask(prompt: str, budget_s: float = 30.0) -> str:
    parts = []
    async with asyncio.timeout(budget_s):  # wall clock for the whole attempt
        stream = await client.chat.completions.create(
            model="gpt-4o-mini", stream=True,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
        async for chunk in stream:
            if chunk.choices and chunk.choices[0].delta.content:
                parts.append(chunk.choices[0].delta.content)
    return "".join(parts)

It raised TimeoutError at 30.0 seconds in both runs this morning; an earlier version of the test ended at 30.0 to 30.1 seconds in three runs. I also checked the socket. Right after the timeout, ss showed no established connection from the client, and the server's next keep-alive write, at 45 seconds, failed with BrokenPipeError. Wrapping the loop in async with stream: made no difference in the same two runs; the cancellation had already closed the connection.

In Sync Code, close() Was 15 Seconds Late

Sync code has no cancellation, so I tried a threading.Timer that fires at 30 seconds. Calling stream.close() from the timer did not interrupt the blocked read. The loop only failed when the next keep-alive arrived, with httpx.ReadError: [Errno 9] Bad file descriptor at 45.4 to 45.5 seconds. So a 30-second deadline ended at 45 seconds. I did not test close() against a silent stream.

Shutting down the socket worked. The timer took the raw socket from stream.response.extensions["network_stream"].get_extra_info("socket") and called shutdown(socket.SHUT_RDWR), and the loop ended at 30.4 to 30.5 seconds over plain HTTP and TLS. That reaches into a low-level httpx response extension, so I would rather move the call into async code or a worker process that can be killed.

Takeaways

  • Treat timeout= on a streamed call as an idle limit. It does not bound how long the attempt runs.
  • Put one wall-clock budget around the request and the iteration together: asyncio.timeout() with AsyncOpenAI.
  • In sync code, stream.close() from another thread waits for the next read. Shut the socket down instead.
  • Around iteration, catch httpx.TimeoutException as well as openai.APITimeoutError.
  • Test against a server that sends one chunk and then only : keep-alive. Mine is 77 lines of standard-library Python, and one run shows whether your deadline holds.

If you run a gateway in front of a model API, does it send comment lines while the model thinks?

articles.title: JavaScript Promises vs Async/Await — Explained Simply
articles.description: I'm Safdar Ali, a frontend engineer in Bengaluru. "Promises vs async await" is not a rivalry —...
articles.body_html:
I'm Safdar Ali, a frontend engineer in Bengaluru. "Promises vs async await" is not a rivalry — async/await is syntax sugar on top of Promises. You still need both mental models for React, Next.js Server Components, and every fetch call. This guide uses BEFORE/AFTER pairs from production code, not toy timers.

Async JavaScript is why frontend engineers touch backends without changing jobs — fetch, auth, file uploads, AI streams. Promises formalised callbacks; async/await made them readable. Search "promises vs async await" and forums still debate syntax preference. In production the debate is error handling and parallelism. Get those right and either syntax works; get them wrong and both fail silently on slow networks in India.

Mental model — pending, fulfilled, rejected

Every Promise is in one of three states. await only pauses inside async functions until fulfillment or rejection. The event loop keeps running other tasks — your loading spinner can animate while fetch waits.

Same async operation — Promise chain vs async/await

type User = { id: string; name: string };


// Promise style

function loadUserPromise(id: string): Promise<User> {

  return fetch("/api/users/" + id)

    .then((res) => {

      if (!res.ok) throw new Error("HTTP " + res.status);

      return res.json() as Promise<User>;

    });

}



// async/await style — identical behavior

async function loadUserAsync(id: string): Promise<User> {

  const res = await fetch("/api/users/" + id);

  if (!res.ok) throw new Error("HTTP " + res.status);

  return res.json() as Promise<User>;

}

Under the hood, async function always returns a Promise. await pauses that function until the Promise settles — it does not block the main thread.

fetch returns a Promise immediately — the HTTP response arrives later. await does not make fetch synchronous; it only pauses your async function until the Promise settles. Other UI keeps updating because the browser event loop is free. That distinction is what interviewers test when they ask about blocking vs non-blocking I/O.

BEFORE / AFTER — escaping callback hell

// BEFORE — nested callbacks (hard to read, easy to miss errors)

getUser(id, (err, user) => {

  if (err) return handle(err);

  getOrders(user.id, (err2, orders) => {

    if (err2) return handle(err2);

    render(user, orders);

  });

});


// AFTER — async/await linear flow

async function showDashboard(id: string) {

  try {

    const user = await loadUserAsync(id);

    const orders = await loadOrders(user.id);

    render(user, orders);

  } catch (err) {

    handle(err);

  }

}

Error handling — try/catch vs .catch()

Style When I use it
try/catch around await Most async functions
.catch() on chain Fire-and-forget analytics
Promise.allSettled Partial failures OK 
// BEFORE — forgot await, try/catch never runs on rejection

async function bad() {

  try {

    const data = fetch("/api/data"); // missing await — bug

    return data;

  } catch (e) {

    console.error(e);

  }

}


// AFTER

async function good() {

  try {

    const res = await fetch("/api/data");

    if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Failed");

    return await res.json();

  } catch (e) {

    console.error(e);

    throw e; // rethrow for UI error boundary

  }

}

Parallel fetch — Promise.all vs sequential await

Sequential await is slow when requests are independent. Dashboard needs user + orders + notifications — run together.

// BEFORE — 3 round trips in series (~900ms total on 300ms each)

async function loadSlow() {

  const user = await fetchUser();

  const orders = await fetchOrders();

  const notes = await fetchNotifications();

  return { user, orders, notes };

}


// AFTER — parallel (~300ms + overhead)

async function loadFast() {

  const [user, orders, notes] = await Promise.all([

    fetchUser(),

    fetchOrders(),

    fetchNotifications(),

  ]);

  return { user, orders, notes };

}
// One failure should not kill all — allSettled

const results = await Promise.allSettled([

  fetchUser(),

  fetchOrders(),

]);

const user = results[0].status === "fulfilled" ? results[0].value : null;

Promise.race is useful for timeouts — reject if fetch exceeds eight seconds on flaky mobile data. Document timeout values in API client modules so the whole app behaves consistently. Sequential await is correct when order matters: create user, then create profile with user id — parallelising those two calls would be a bug.

Next.js Server Components — async by default

// app/dashboard/page.tsx

type Stats = { users: number; revenue: number };


async function getStats(): Promise<Stats> {

  const res = await fetch("https://api.example.com/stats", {

    next: { revalidate: 60 },

  });

  if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Stats unavailable");

  return res.json();

}



export default async function DashboardPage() {

  const stats = await getStats();

  return <StatsPanel stats={stats} />;

}

Server Components are async functions — no useEffect fetch. See RSC vs client components.

Client pitfalls — useEffect and race conditions

// BEFORE — no abort, stale response overwrites new search

useEffect(() => {

  fetch("/api/search?q=" + query).then((r) => r.json()).then(setResults);

}, [query]);


// AFTER — AbortController

useEffect(() => {

  const ctrl = new AbortController();

  (async () => {

    try {

      const res = await fetch("/api/search?q=" + query, { signal: ctrl.signal });

      const data = await res.json();

      setResults(data);

    } catch (e) {

      if ((e as Error).name !== "AbortError") console.error(e);

    }

  })();

  return () => ctrl.abort();

}, [query]);

Promises vs async/await — quick comparison

Topic Promises (.then) async/await
Readability Chains indent right Linear top-to-bottom
Error handling .catch() at end try/catch around await
Parallelism Promise.all([...]) await Promise.all([...])
Return type Always Promise async fn returns Promise
Debugging Stack in .then Stack at await line

When I keep raw Promises

Utility libraries returning Promises, combining with Promise.race for timeouts, or .then() in non-async callbacks. async/await is for readable control flow; Promises are the underlying contract.

Creating Promises — wrap legacy callbacks once

function readFileAsync(path: string): Promise<string> {

  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {

    readFile(path, "utf8", (err, data) => {

      if (err) reject(err);

      else resolve(data);

    });

  });

}


// Prefer promisify utilities in Node; in browser wrap once at module boundary

Async iterators — streams beyond one JSON blob

async function* lineChunks(stream: ReadableStream<Uint8Array>) {

  const reader = stream.getReader();

  const decoder = new TextDecoder();

  let buffer = "";

  while (true) {

    const { done, value } = await reader.read();

    if (done) break;

    buffer += decoder.decode(value, { stream: true });

    const lines = buffer.split("\n");

    buffer = lines.pop() ?? "";

    for (const line of lines) yield line;

  }

}

Large CSV exports and AI streaming responses use async iteration. Promises handle single results; iterators handle sequences. Both compose with await in for-await-of loops.

Unhandled rejections — the production alert you want

// Node / edge — log unhandled rejections in API routes

process.on("unhandledRejection", (reason) => {

  console.error("Unhandled rejection:", reason);

});


// Always return Response from route handlers — never floating promise

export async function GET() {

  try {

    const data = await loadData();

    return Response.json(data);

  } catch (e) {

    return Response.json({ error: "Server error" }, { status: 500 });

  }

}

Floating promises in server actions and API routes caused silent 500s on a client project until we wrapped every async entry point. Treat await like a return statement — every path must settle.

Practice pattern

Rewrite one sequential useEffect fetch as Promise.all. Add try/catch and rethrow. Measure network tab — the win is immediate on slow Indian mobile networks.

Async literacy is the bridge between UI work and API design. When you read backend OpenAPI docs, you already think in Promises — negotiating timeout and retry policies with your team gets easier.

The syntax debate ends when you debug: stack traces from async/await point at your await line; Promise chains point at the nearest .then. Pick whichever makes the failure obvious to your future self.

Server Actions in Next.js return Promises to the client when you call them from forms — same mental model, different wire format. Always handle rejection in UI with error boundaries or toast messages; unhandled rejections in the browser console are user-facing failures you never measured.

Next: JavaScript array methods. Performance: web performance checklist.

Async patterns in React 19 and Next.js 15 still bottom out on Promises — Suspense boundaries await async children, error boundaries catch rejections. When you wrap a component in Suspense, you are telling React a Promise will resolve with UI. The syntax changed; the contract did not. Learn Promise.all before learning Server Actions — the same parallelism rules apply server-side.

Testing async code: use async test functions in Vitest, await expect(loadUser()).resolves.toMatchObject(...). Mock fetch at module level for API units; integration tests hit MSW handlers. Flaky tests often come from missing await or shared mutable state between tests — isolate with beforeEach resets.

Indian mobile networks add packet loss — always set fetch timeouts and show retry UI. Users blame your app, not Jio. Log failed requests with correlation ids in API routes so support can trace one user complaint to one server log line. Async without observability is debugging with eyes closed.

Dynamic import() returns a Promise — lazy routes in React and Next.js use it under the hood. await import() in event handlers loads code on demand; do not confuse with static import at top of file. Error boundaries catch render failures; import().catch handles load failures for chunks — handle both in production apps with friendly fallback UI.

Microtask queue education: await schedules continuations as microtasks; setTimeout is macrotask. Ordering bugs appear when mixing them in tests — flushPromises helpers in test utils exist for a reason. Read MDN event loop once; every async interview question becomes easier.

Promises vs async/await is not a style war — it is one runtime model. Write async/await in application code, read Promise chains in library source, debug both in stack traces. Ship one refactor this sprint: parallelise three serial fetches and measure waterfall in Network tab. The milliseconds you save are user trust earned.

Copy these BEFORE/AFTER blocks into your team wiki — replace URLs with internal APIs. New hires in India often learn async from YouTube shorts that skip error handling; this article is the correction layer before they touch production checkout flows.

finally blocks run after try/catch regardless of success — use for cleanup (revoke object URLs, set loading false). Do not return values from finally that override try return — confusing control flow. Keep finally boring: flags and cleanup only.

Async generators and for await...of handle streams of chunks — payment webhooks, log tailing, SSE. Promises return one value; iterators return many. Learn for await after mastering Promise.all — not before.

Top-level await in ES modules runs at import time — powerful in Node scripts, dangerous in client bundles that block parse. Next.js restricts patterns; follow framework docs. When in doubt, await inside async functions you call from entry points you control.

Save this article for code review — when you see .then().then().then(), suggest async/await refactor in a follow-up PR. When you see missing await, block merge. Async bugs are P0 in payment flows; style issues can wait, correctness cannot.

Promises vs async await is the same language at different readability levels — master both, ship fewer bugs, and explain your Next.js data layer in interviews without hand-waving. That is the whole goal of this guide from Bengaluru production work, not syntax trivia. Re-read the parallel fetch BEFORE/AFTER before your next dashboard page ships.

Promises vs async await confusion usually hides one bug: missing await, serial fetch, or swallowed rejection. Fix those three patterns and most async incidents disappear from your on-call rotation — more valuable than debating syntax preference in Slack threads that never ship code.

Open Network tab, find three serial fetches, parallelise with Promise.all, measure — that ten-minute exercise is worth more than rereading this paragraph. Promises vs async await only matters when milliseconds and error paths reach real users on real networks in India and everywhere else your app ships.

Server Actions return Promises to the client when invoked from forms — handle pending and error UI explicitly. Route handlers must await every async call before returning Response — floating promises caused silent failures on a fintech project I debugged in Bengaluru until we added integration tests that assert status codes. Async literacy is not optional for full-stack frontend roles in 2026; it is the baseline.

Copy the BEFORE/AFTER blocks into your codebase as comments above legacy fetch code — future refactors will thank you. Delete the comments after refactor ships. Promises vs async await is maintenance work, not a one-time read ever.
