articles.title: I measured my auto video editor on real streams. It was picking the outro.
articles.description: I build Phoenix Editor, a desktop app that takes a long stream or Let's Play recording, cuts the dead...
articles.body_html:
I build Phoenix Editor, a desktop app that takes a long stream or Let's Play recording, cuts the dead air and filler words, and turns the best moments into captioned vertical Shorts. It runs on your own GPU: faster-whisper on NVIDIA, whisper.cpp over Vulkan on AMD and Intel, and the encoder your card has.

For months the test suite ran it against generated fixtures, and everything passed. Then someone called it "vibecoded slop" in public, and I realised I had no evidence they were wrong. Nothing in the repo showed the edits were actually good on real footage.

So I built a harness, ran it on real commentary, and wrote down what came back. This post is the numbers, the bugs they exposed, and the fixes.

The harness

Scoring an edit is harder than it sounds, because "good" is subjective. I picked things I could measure:

  • Words lost. Transcribe the source with a separate model (Whisper medium.en, word timestamps). Any reference word that falls inside a removed range was cut by mistake.
  • Words clipped. A cut boundary that lands inside a word, so the edit says "basi-" and jumps.
  • Fillers removed. Reference "um"s and "uh"s that are actually gone from the render.
  • What the Shorts picker chose, checked by watching them.

The test set was CC-BY and CC-BY-SA videos from archive.org and similar, uploaded by the people who made them:

Length Kind
A raw Twitch stream 3h 09m VTuber overlay, horror RPG
An FPS first-impressions video 20m facecam, lightly edited
A two-player strategy game 11m two voices
Two Let's Play episodes 50m each no commentary at all

The two with no commentary were a free check: the engine should refuse them rather than "edit" a silent video. It did.

Round one

3h stream FPS strategy
Removed 63 of 189 min 5.7 of 20 min 2.3 of 11 min
Reference words lost 4.1% 1.8% 2.5%
Words with a cut inside them 2.6% 1.7% 2.4%
Fillers removed 2 of 19 2 of 36 3 of 8

Losing one word in 25 sounds small until you watch it. Every lost word came from a silence cut. About 60% sat within 0.4 s of a cut edge, so the padding was too tight. The rest were deep inside a "silence" that wasn't: quiet speech under game audio.

The fillers were worse, and the cause was not my code. Whisper doesn't write "um" and "uh" by default. It cleans them out of the transcript, and a filler detector that reads the transcript can't cut what isn't there.

And the Shorts were bad enough to be funny:

  • On the 3-hour stream, all five Shorts came from the first eight minutes: pre-game chat about having a cold. None from the two boss fights the stream was named after.
  • On the FPS video, three of five were the outro.
  • On the strategy video, the intro and the outro.

Why the Shorts picker failed

The first version scored fixed 15-second windows on a 5-second grid by loudness and words per second. That rewards exactly the wrong thing. When does a streamer talk fast and loud? When they're explaining something to the camera: the intro, the outro, the sponsor bit. When something actually happens in the game, they react: "oh", "no no no", "wait", "let's go". Short bursts, not monologue.

And a grid window starts and ends wherever the grid says, which is mid-sentence.

The fixes

Cut edges. Silence cuts now stop short of every transcribed word: 80 ms before it, 120 ms after. One subtle bug on the way: there's a cap on how long a silence cut can be, and it was judged after carving out words. A quiet half hour with one word in it got chopped into dozens of jump cuts, removing 504 s instead of 171. The cap is now judged on the whole pause first.

Fillers. Whisper can be told to write them: hotwords on faster-whisper, an initial prompt on whisper.cpp. That worked, with a catch: primed to hear "uh", it also hears some short real words as "uh". Measured against the reference transcript, the culprits were the low-confidence ones and the implausibly long ones (a 3-second "uh" is a stretched timestamp over real speech). So a filler is only cut when Whisper is at least 40% sure and it's at most 1.2 s long. Leaving an "um" in is cheaper than cutting a word.

There was a second filler bug, and it's my favourite: the fillers that were detected mostly never left the render. The pause padding, scene snapping and word guards that protect speech were also erasing the tiny filler cuts. Only 6 of 27 detected fillers made it out. Filler cuts now skip those steps and keep a 40 ms margin.

Repetition loops. Turning on hotwords together with conditioning on previous text locked faster-whisper into repeating one line from minute 70 of the 3-hour stream to the end: 386 words where there should have been about 1,500. Conditioning is off now, and both backends collapse runs of four or more identical sentences.

Shorts, rebuilt:

  1. Clips are built from whole sentences, 20 to 45 seconds, so a Short opens on a thought and closes on one.
  2. The main signal is reaction density, not talk. Loudness and speech rate only count relative to the speaker's own level a few minutes either side, so someone who is loud all night doesn't win everywhere.
  3. A vision pass labels scenes. Combat and cutscenes add to a clip; menus, loading screens and idle subtract.
  4. Intros, outros and "links in the description" are ruled out, and the first and last couple of minutes of a long recording are discounted.
  5. Picks are spread out, with a minimum gap that scales with the recording's length. And if there aren't five good moments, you get fewer Shorts rather than filler.

The layout changed too. On a facecam recording, the old reframer followed the face, so the 9:16 crop was the webcam corner and the gameplay was cropped away. Now the facecam is found (YuNet plus edge refinement) and stacked above the gameplay, with 2 to 3 word captions at the seam.

Round two

FPS before FPS after strategy before strategy after
Reference words lost 1.8% 0.99% 2.5% 0.22%
Words with a cut inside them 1.7% 1.36% 2.4% 1.25%
Fillers removed from the render ~2 20 of 27 detected ~3 3 of 5 detected

The Shorts on the FPS video are now five gameplay reactions ("whoa whoa whoa", "it feels like a war zone", "just ate a grenade"). The strategy video gets four mid-game moments.

What's still weak

The raw 3-hour VTuber stream. The avatar has no face to stack, the vision pass mislabels an intermission card as gameplay, and some of the transcribed speech is game dialogue rather than the streamer. Those picks are still poor, and I'd rather say so than pretend.

The filler confidence gate also only works on the NVIDIA path for now, because whisper.cpp's per-word confidence isn't wired in yet.

What I'd tell anyone building something similar

  • Test on real footage early. Generated fixtures tested that the code ran. They couldn't tell me it picked the outro.
  • Score against an independent transcript. If you score your edit with the same transcript you used to make it, every mistake is invisible.
  • Whisper's defaults are tuned for clean text, not editing. If you need disfluencies, ask for them, then filter what comes back.
  • "Loud and fast" is not "exciting". Reactions are.

Phoenix Editor runs on Windows and Linux, on AMD or NVIDIA, and nothing uploads. There's a 7-day free trial with every feature and no watermark, and a setup guide if you want to throw a VOD at it. If it picks your outro, tell me.

articles.title: One Month After the Hackathon: Why My 4-Service App Stopped Working (and What @mansio Caught in the Verifiers)
articles.description: What breaks a month after a hackathon, and what a fellow DEV writer caught in the verifiers.   TL;DR:...
articles.body_html:
What breaks a month after a hackathon, and what a fellow DEV writer caught in the verifiers.

TL;DR: A month after shipping README Clew 2, I opened it up and every scan failed. Nothing was wrong with the deterministic verifiers or with Jev on Glasser. Instead, three small operational traps lined up at once: an expired 30-day GitHub token on a tool that only reads public repos, a rotated Claude Haiku key scoped only to Development in Vercel, and a substring bug that fellow DEV writer Mikhail (@mansio) found and fixed in PR #2.

In October I built README Clew 2 for the AdaL "What Would Jev Do?" hackathon. It checks whether a public JavaScript or TypeScript repo's README matches its code, sorting every checkable line into four buckets: Contradicted, Missing, Unverifiable, and Verified.

The core rule of the build is that models never decide what is true:

Job Who does it
Split the README into lines and settle obvious headings/badges Deterministic code rules
Label what kind of claim a prose line makes (command, dependency, env var, file/URL) Jev (jev-1.13.0) via Glasser, gated at 0.8 confidence
Decide Verified, Contradicted, or Missing Five deterministic code verifiers
Write a two-sentence plain-English summary from the counts Claude Haiku (claude-haiku-5-5), fail-open

When you wire that many moving parts together (AdaL, Jev, Glasser, Haiku, GitHub, and Vercel) and come back a month later to a red SCAN FAILED banner, it is hard to tell at first glance which piece broke.

Here is what was actually wrong, and the two fixes that came out of it.

1. When "javascript" hides "ava": @mansio's PR #2

Before I even got to the deployment keys, Mikhail (@mansio) had opened and landed PR #2, the project's first external code contribution.

Mikhail was testing README Clew 2 against real repositories and noticed something strange on sindresorhus/yocto-queue. The repo uses ava as a test runner, and the README never mentions ava. The coverage verifier should have flagged ava in the Missing bucket. Instead, it stayed silent.

Why? Because the README contained a link to Mozilla's documentation:

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Iteration_protocols

And inside the word javascript, in lowercase, sits the three-letter substring ava.

Our coverage check was using a plain substring match:

// Before: any substring match counted as "mentioned in the README"
if (readme.includes(name.toLowerCase())) continue;

Even worse, the same substring check lived in the dependency verifier's prose guard (inCodeContext), which checks whether a candidate package name appears on an install line. A short name like can inside npm i canvas-parser or lodash inside npm i lodash-es could bypass the prose guard and reach Contradicted, the exact false positive the guard was built to prevent.

The fix

Mikhail replaced both substring checks with a single whole-token rule, mentionsWord(), bounded by npm's own package name characters (A-Za-z0-9_-) plus @ and /:

export function mentionsWord(text, name) {
  if (!name) return false;
  const esc = name.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&');
  return new RegExp(`(?<![A-Za-z0-9_@/-])${esc}(?![A-Za-z0-9_-])`, 'i').test(text);
}

With that in place:

  • We use ava. and Tests run with \ava. still count as real mentions.
  • mozilla.org/.../javascript/... no longer hides ava.
  • npm i lodash-es no longer treats lodash as an installed package claim.

Mikhail shipped the fix with a 27-case test matrix and verifier controls in tests/mentions-word.test.js, matching the repo's file-size cap and offline test rules on the first try. If you have not read his engineering field notes on DEV (like The Dataset Was Lying: 4 of 6 "False" Facts Were True), go read him.

2. The 30-day time bomb: sending an expired token to a public API

Once Mikhail's PR was merged, I still had a live site that refused to scan.

Every click on SCAN returned HTTP 502:

{"error":{"code":"github_forbidden","message":"GitHub returned HTTP 401"}}

The ironic part: README Clew 2 only scans public repositories. It makes 4 metadata calls to api.github.com per scan and fetches the files from raw.githubusercontent.com. You do not even need a GITHUB_TOKEN for low-volume public reads (GitHub allows 60 unauthenticated REST calls per hour per IP, or 15 full scans per hour).

During the October hackathon, I had added a 30-day GitHub Personal Access Token so repeated test scans wouldn't hit the unauthenticated rate limit. Thirty days passed, the token expired, and lib/github.js kept sending Authorization: Bearer <expired_token> on every request.

GitHub allows requests with no Authorization header, but immediately rejects requests carrying an expired Authorization header with 401 Bad credentials. Because step 1 threw a GithubError, the pipeline stopped before Jev or Haiku ever ran.

The 4-line fix

First, I removed the expired GITHUB_TOKEN from Vercel. Second, we hardened lib/github.js so that if an expired token is ever present in .env or server environment variables and GitHub answers 401, the client drops the authorization header from the shared headers object and retries unauthenticated:

if (res.status === 401 && headers?.authorization) {
  delete headers.authorization; // expired or bad token: public repos work without it
  return request(url, { fetchImpl, headers, as });
}

Because headers is shared across the 4 metadata calls in fetchRepo(), dropping headers.authorization on the first 401 means the remaining 3 calls go straight out without the bad token.

3. Silent fail-open + Vercel environment scopes

The last piece was Claude Haiku. By design, Haiku is fail-open in README Clew 2: if the summary call fails or times out, the report still renders in full and the clew mascot falls back to a fixed one-line summary per mood.

My October Anthropic key had also been rotated. When I added the new ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in Vercel, two classic traps bit me at the same time:

  1. The new key was scoped to Development in Vercel, while Production and Preview still held the 34-day-old key.
  2. Vercel environment variable changes only take effect on the next deployment.

Running vercel env ls made the split visible right away:

Variable Environment Created
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (new) Development Today
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (old) Production, Preview 34d ago
GLASSER_API_KEY Production, Preview, Development 34d ago

Overriding ANTHROPIC_API_KEY across all three environments (Production, Preview, Development) and running vercel --prod brought the Haiku summary and bucket notes back on the first scan. Meanwhile, Glasser and Jev (jev-1.13.0) never missed a beat: all 4 batched calls completed in 1.37 seconds for about half a cent ($0.0055), with $10.80 of the original hackathon balance still untouched.

Related reading on DEV

Two posts from the community hit the exact operational edges from today's debugging session:

  • ["Invalid API key" or undefined env vars on Vercel: how to fix it] by @unbreakkit walks through how environment variable scopes (Production vs Preview vs Development) and missing redeploys cause 401 Invalid API key errors on Vercel even after you paste a fresh key.
  • [Your AI Agent Runs for Hours. Its GitHub Token Might Not.] by @__be2942592 looks at what happens when code assumes a GitHub token in the environment is valid forever instead of handling 401 expiration explicitly.

Try it

  • Live page: readme-clew-2.vercel.app (click USE DEMO REPO, then SCAN)
  • Source and 478 offline tests: github.com/earlgreyhot1701D/readme-clew-2

Thank you again to Mikhail (@mansio) for finding the substring bug on a real repo and shipping a clean, well-tested fix.

Quick context if you are new here. I work in the California courts, running court operations for the county. I started building with AI in July 2025 and I have been learning in public ever since. I do not write the code. I direct, the agents generate, I validate and decide. I build the Clew Suite, a set of civic tech tools for making complex systems easier to inspect. That is the lens I am writing from.

AI Assisted. Human Approved. Powered by NLP.

articles.title: Build an Offline AI Study App with Local Models (Liquid AI LFM3-1.7B)
articles.description: I ran Liquid AI's LFM3-1.7B in the browser with WebGPU and built Grading Buddy, an offline study app that answers only from notes I've checked.
articles.body_html:
Hey everyone. Today I want to show you how you can use local models, using Liquid AI's LFM3, their latest model.

What local models are

First of all, what does a local model mean? It means a model that is on your device. You download it, and it runs on your device. So you don't need a connection to the internet, you don't need to spend any money because it's free and on your device, and everything stays private. There are a lot of benefits to using local models.

A minimal LFM3 chat in the browser

Let me show you a very simple example. I built a very small chat app, about 45 lines of code, just to show how easily you can get started. I'm getting Transformers.js from Hugging Face, then there's my model, and I'm using WebGPU so it runs in the browser. That's basically all you need to build something like this. I told you it was minimal.

Then you ask your question: what is the capital of France? It downloads the model, the model is now running on my device, it's not going to the cloud and it's not costing me any money. The capital of France is Paris. I can change that to Ireland, and I get Dublin, really fast.

The tech, in plain words

Before we go further, here's what's actually going on in that tiny page.

  • LFM3-1.7B is Liquid AI's small text model in the LFM3 family. Small enough to run on a laptop, and good at following "answer only from these facts" instructions. I use the ONNX export on Hugging Face, which is the version made to run in a browser. You can read more on the model card and in Liquid's docs.
  • Transformers.js is Hugging Face's JavaScript library for running models in the browser. It downloads the model and runs it for you, so you don't need a server.
  • WebGPU is the browser API that lets a web page use your computer's graphics card. A model does a lot of maths, and the GPU does it much faster than the CPU. That's why the app needs a desktop browser with WebGPU, like Chrome or Edge.

Loading the model

This is the heart of the minimal page. One import, one pipeline, then you ask it a question:

import { pipeline } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@huggingface/transformers@4.3.2";

const chat = await pipeline("text-generation", "onnx-community/LFM3-1.7B-ONNX", {
  dtype: "q4f16",
  device: "webgpu",
});

const out = await chat(
  [
    { role: "system", content: "You are a helpful assistant. Answer briefly." },
    { role: "user", content: "What is the capital of France?" },
  ],
  { max_new_tokens: 150, do_sample: false, tokenizer_encode_kwargs: { enable_thinking: false } },
);

q4f16 is a compressed version of the model, which keeps the download to about 1.1 GB. device: "webgpu" runs it on the GPU. enable_thinking: false turns off LFM3's thinking so you get a direct answer. The whole page is in examples/minimal in the repo.

What gets downloaded and cached

The first time you press Download and start, the browser fetches the model files from Hugging Face, about 1.1 GB, just once. Transformers.js keeps them in the browser's cache, and in the full app (more on that below) a service worker caches the app itself. So after that first download it works with no internet at all.

How the app works

The full app wraps the model in a few simple steps:

  1. Topic match. It picks the grading topic that best fits your question.
  2. Say no early. If nothing matches, the app tells you it's not part of the grading and doesn't call the model at all.
  3. Give the model the notes. LFM3 gets that topic's facts and answers in a sentence or two.
  4. Check the answer. A grounding check (Korean terms, numbers, type of answer) and a required-facts check both have to pass.
  5. Fall back to the note. If either check fails, you see the note card labelled From the notes instead.

The model runs in a Web Worker so the page doesn't freeze while it thinks. Liquid's own docs say "Use retrieval or search for knowledge-heavy tasks", and that's exactly why the facts come from my notes and not from the model's memory.

Where a small model falls short

Now, what if I ask what Chon-Ji means? I'm studying for my Taekwon-Do grading, so that's a real question for me. It told me Chon-Ji is a Buddhist temple in Kyoto, Japan. No, it's not. Chon-Ji means heaven and earth.

And when I asked what the tenets of Taekwon-Do are, it didn't give me the answer.

That's the problem with local models. Sometimes they don't have enough knowledge, and you think, right, this is not good enough, I need a bigger model and I'll just pay for it. But no. You can use local models in so many other ways.

Giving the model your own notes

So the minimal version proved the model runs on my device, fast and for free. It just didn't know Taekwon-Do. And that's what I actually needed help with for my grading. So I went and built a proper app around it, called Grading Buddy. It's a study app that only answers from notes I've checked, and tells you when something isn't part of the grading.

I could have fine-tuned the model and shown it more Taekwon-Do. Instead, what I'm doing is giving it a content.json file with extra content about Taekwon-Do. It's the same content I use on the website to show that information. Then the chat part lets students ask their questions about Taekwon-Do and get the correct answers.

Grading Buddy: Ask, answered on device

So this is the app, Grading Buddy, with everything about Chon-Ji, the belts, the tenets and the rest. If I ask "what are the five tenets?", I get courtesy, integrity, perseverance, self-control and indomitable spirit. That answer was written by LFM3 on this device.

I can also see how it was answered. That's built in for this demo, and you wouldn't want it in the real app. But you can see the path, that it used the model, how long it took, and the checks it needed to pass to get to that answer.

When an answer check fails

Next I asked how many moves are in Chon-Ji. It thought about it, and then it couldn't answer. So what happened? The panel shows it failed on a missing required fact. So we can look in our notes, the JSON file, and find out why that check failed and which notes are missing. Then, rather than fine-tuning the model, we fine-tune the notes so it can get the answer to that question.

Then I asked how to count to ten in Korean, and that answer came from the model on this device too. And when I asked my first question again, what does Chon-Ji mean, I got heaven and earth, the first pattern you learn.

So that's how you can use a local model in your app to do some really fun things. People type their questions and get answers based on the knowledge you give it.

Quiz and Learn why

You can do some extra fun things too. In the quiz, one question was which part of the foot you use for a front snap kick. I put the heel, which is totally wrong. It's the ball of the foot. That feedback comes straight from the notes, in simple words. But you can also click Learn why, and the explanation is a little bit nicer: a front snap kick is called apcha busigi, you lift the knee, and it's a strong kick to the front. Just some extra wording in there, and I quite like it.

That could be really nice when you're helping children learn. The model can make your answers a little more fun and friendly. On another question, the Learn why explanation walked through the end of the pattern, steps 17, 18 and 19, and bringing the left foot back to parallel stance. That's really helpful, and much nicer than just saying yes, it's right.

Try it yourself

So that's what you can do with local models. That's Liquid AI's LFM3, and I've made the app open source, so go and check it out, download it and play around with it. The README is very simple: git clone, cd into the folder, npm ci, npm run dev, then ask those questions and build something yourself. Check out the minimal file too if you want to. Local models are very cool and worth trying out. So go build something cool, and have fun.

  • Grading Buddy repo
  • Live app (desktop browser with WebGPU)
  • LFM3-1.7B on Hugging Face
  • Transformers.js
  • Liquid AI

articles.title: React `useId` in 2026: Why It Beats `Math.random()` for Accessibility and SSR Hydration
articles.description: Learn why React's useId Hook solves SSR hydration mismatches and accessibility problems that Math.random() and crypto.randomUUID() cannot fix. Includes production patterns and common pitfalls.
articles.body_html:
React useId in 2026: Why It Beats Math.random() for Accessibility and SSR Hydration

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Most React developers reach for Math.random() when they need a unique ID. The component renders, the form field gets an ID, the label connects, and everything works. Ship it.

Then the production SSR logs fill with hydration warnings. Screen readers stop announcing field relationships. The client DOM re-renders on every page load, flickering inputs and breaking focus states. Users file accessibility bugs, and the team scrambles to find the root cause.

The problem is not random IDs themselves. The problem is that Math.random() runs twice in server-side rendering: once on the server, once on the client. Two separate JavaScript runtimes produce two different values for the same component instance. React expects the HTML to match between renders, discovers a mismatch, and throws a hydration error.

React's useId Hook (introduced in React 18.0.0, documented at react.dev/reference/react/useId) solves this by generating deterministic IDs that match across server and client boundaries. The server emits ":r1:", the client hydrates with ":r1:", and the DOM stays intact.

This post explains the technical mechanism, shows production patterns for accessible forms, compares useId against alternatives, and documents the edge cases where developers should avoid it entirely.

Key Takeaways

  • useId generates stable IDs that match between server and client renders, eliminating SSR hydration mismatches.
  • Random ID generators (Math.random(), crypto.randomUUID()) break hydration because they produce different values on each runtime.
  • The Hook creates accessibility relationships (aria-describedby, aria-labelledby) that persist across renders without causing warnings.
  • Developers should never use useId for React list keys or cache keys (both require data-derived identifiers, not component-instance IDs).
  • Production components can call useId multiple times or concatenate a shared prefix to generate related IDs for complex form patterns.

The SSR Hydration Mismatch Problem

Server-side rendering sends HTML to the browser before JavaScript loads. React then hydrates that HTML by attaching event handlers and verifying the DOM structure matches what the component would render on the client.

When an ID changes between server and client renders, React logs a warning and replaces the server HTML with a new client render. This destroys form state, breaks focus, and forces a layout shift.

The sequence happens in milliseconds but produces user-visible defects. A password field loses focus. A screen reader announces the wrong hint text. The browser re-paints the form, causing a flicker.

// This breaks SSR hydration
function BrokenPasswordField() {
  const hintId = `hint-${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2)}`;

  return (
    <>
      <label>
        Password:
        <input type="password" aria-describedby={hintId} />
      </label>
      <p id={hintId}>Must contain at least 18 characters</p>
    </>
  );
}

The server renders hint-abc123. The client renders hint-xyz789. React sees the mismatch in the id and aria-describedby attributes, discards the server HTML, and re-renders from scratch on the client. Console logs show:

Warning: Prop `id` did not match. Server: "hint-abc123" Client: "hint-xyz789"

The root issue is that Math.random() is non-deterministic across JavaScript runtimes. Node.js (server) and the browser (client) use different random number generators seeded differently. Even if they used the same algorithm, there is no guarantee the sequence would align because other code might consume random values between component renders.

Developers sometimes attempt to fix this by moving the ID generation into useEffect, which only runs on the client. This eliminates the hydration mismatch but introduces a worse problem: the server HTML ships without any id attribute, so the aria-describedby reference points to nothing. Screen readers cannot find the hint text. The component works for sighted users but fails accessibility requirements.

Diagram showing SSR hydration flow with mismatched IDs

How useId Generates Stable IDs Across Server and Client

React's useId Hook produces IDs based on the component's position in the tree, not on random values or execution order. The official React 18 release notes describe the mechanism: "Inside React, useId is generated from the 'parent path' of the calling component."

Each component in the React tree has an implicit path from the root. When a component calls useId, React concatenates the path segments into a deterministic string. The same component in the same tree position always gets the same ID, regardless of whether the code runs on the server or the client.

function StablePasswordField() {
  const hintId = useId();

  return (
    <>
      <label>
        Password:
        <input type="password" aria-describedby={hintId} />
      </label>
      <p id={hintId}>Must contain at least 18 characters</p>
    </>
  );
}

On the server, useId returns ":r1:". On the client, hydration assigns ":r1:" to the same component instance. The id and aria-describedby attributes match. React skips the re-render and preserves the server HTML.

The ID format includes a colon prefix to ensure it does not conflict with developer-defined IDs. The alphanumeric suffix encodes the component's tree position in a compact form. If the same component renders twice in the tree, each instance gets a distinct ID because each occupies a different position.

This tree-based generation has a critical constraint: the component tree must be identical on the server and the client. If a component conditionally renders based on client-only state (window width, local storage, cookies), the tree structure diverges and useId produces different IDs. The useId documentation explicitly warns: "With server rendering, useId requires an identical component tree on the server and the client."

Developers working with multiple React applications on a single HTML page can set the identifierPrefix option in createRoot or hydrateRoot (as documented in the React 18 release notes) to namespace the IDs and prevent collisions between apps. The prefix prepends to every useId result within that root.

Building Accessible Form Components with useId

Accessible forms require explicit relationships between labels, inputs, error messages, and hint text. ARIA attributes like aria-describedby and aria-labelledby reference element IDs to build those relationships, documented in the MDN ARIA guide.

A production-ready form field needs a unique ID for the input, a unique ID for the hint text, and optionally a unique ID for error messages. The useId Hook provides a stable base that developers can extend with suffixes.

import { useId, useState } from 'react';

function EmailField() {
  const baseId = useId();
  const inputId = `${baseId}-input`;
  const hintId = `${baseId}-hint`;
  const errorId = `${baseId}-error`;

  const [email, setEmail] = useState('');
  const [error, setError] = useState('');

  const validateEmail = (value: string) => {
    if (!value.includes('@')) {
      setError('Email must contain an @ symbol');
    } else {
      setError('');
    }
  };

  return (
    <div>
      <label htmlFor={inputId}>
        Email Address
      </label>
      <input
        id={inputId}
        type="email"
        value={email}
        onChange={(e) => {
          setEmail(e.target.value);
          validateEmail(e.target.value);
        }}
        aria-describedby={error ? errorId : hintId}
        aria-invalid={!!error}
      />
      {error ? (
        <p id={errorId} role="alert">
          {error}
        </p>
      ) : (
        <p id={hintId}>
          We will never share your email
        </p>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

This pattern creates a stable foundation for component libraries. A TextField component can call useId internally and expose the IDs through props if consumers need to reference them externally. The IDs never change across renders unless the component unmounts and remounts in a different tree position.

Screen readers announce the hint text when the input receives focus, then switch to the error message if validation fails. The aria-invalid attribute signals the error state to assistive technology. All relationships remain intact because the IDs are deterministic and match between server and client.

Developers building forms with libraries like React Hook Form or Formik can integrate useId into custom field components while letting the library handle validation and state management. The pattern described in useFormStatus and useFormState for accessible forms combines server actions with useId for full-stack form handling.

Accessible form field showing label, input, and hint text with aria relationships

Math.random() vs useId vs crypto.randomUUID(): The Complete Comparison

Developers choosing an ID generation strategy face three common options: Math.random(), crypto.randomUUID(), and useId. Each has different tradeoffs for collision probability, SSR compatibility, and browser support.

Approach SSR Safe Collision Risk Browser Support Use Case
Math.random() No Medium (birthday paradox applies) Universal Client-only apps with no SSR
crypto.randomUUID() No Negligible (128-bit UUID) Modern browsers only (requires secure context) Secure client-only tokens
useId Yes None within a React tree React 18+ Accessibility IDs in SSR apps

Math.random() generates a floating-point number between 0 and 1, which developers typically convert to a string with .toString(36).slice(2). This produces short alphanumeric strings but does not guarantee uniqueness. The birthday paradox means collisions become likely after a few thousand IDs.

crypto.randomUUID() (introduced in WHATWG Secure Contexts) generates RFC 4122 version 4 UUIDs with 128 bits of entropy. Collisions are astronomically unlikely. However, the function requires a secure context (HTTPS or localhost) and is unavailable in older browsers and some Node.js environments. More importantly, it runs independently on the server and client, producing different UUIDs and breaking hydration exactly like Math.random().

useId does not aim for cryptographic security or global uniqueness. It guarantees uniqueness within a single React component tree and stability across server and client renders. The IDs are short (typically 3-5 characters) and readable in DevTools. For accessibility attributes, this is the correct tradeoff: developers need deterministic, collision-free IDs that survive hydration, not UUIDs that resist brute-force attacks.

Developers sometimes combine approaches: generate a UUID on the server, store it in component state, and reference it in accessibility attributes. This works but adds unnecessary complexity. The UUID never leaves the component, so cryptographic security provides no benefit. The state update forces an extra render. useId solves the same problem with zero client-side state and zero re-renders.

Common useId Pitfalls: When NOT to Use It

The official useId documentation lists two explicit anti-patterns: "should not be used to generate keys in a list" and "should not be used to generate cache keys."

React list keys must be stable across re-renders and tied to the underlying data. A key like user-${user.id} lets React track which user moved when the list re-orders. A key from useId changes when the component remounts, causing React to destroy and recreate DOM nodes unnecessarily.

// WRONG: useId for list keys
function UserList({ users }: { users: User[] }) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {users.map((user) => {
        const id = useId(); // Creates a new ID on every render
        return <li key={id}>{user.name}</li>;
      })}
    </ul>
  );
}

// CORRECT: Use data as the key source
function UserList({ users }: { users: User[] }) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {users.map((user) => (
        <li key={user.id}>{user.name}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

Cache keys have a similar requirement: they must derive from the data being cached, not from the component requesting it. If two components request the same data, they should use the same cache key. useId generates different IDs for different component instances, so each instance would create a separate cache entry for identical data.

The React 18 release notes also mention that useId "currently cannot be used in async Server Components." Server Components (as described in the experimental React Server Components RFC) suspend during render to fetch data. React cannot determine the component's tree position until the suspension resolves, so useId cannot generate a stable path-based ID.

Developers building Jotai atomic state or similar libraries should not use useId to identify atoms. Atom identity must persist across component unmounts and remounts. useId ties to the component lifecycle, so an atom identified by useId would lose its state when the component unmounts.

Production Patterns: Multiple IDs in a Single Component

Complex form controls often need multiple related IDs. A combobox requires an ID for the input, an ID for the listbox, and IDs for each option. A date picker needs IDs for the input, the calendar popup, and potentially each date cell.

The official useId documentation shows the recommended pattern: "If you need to give IDs to multiple related elements, you can call useId to generate a shared prefix for them."

import { useId } from 'react';

function Combobox({ options }: { options: string[] }) {
  const baseId = useId();
  const inputId = `${baseId}-input`;
  const listboxId = `${baseId}-listbox`;

  return (
    <div>
      <label htmlFor={inputId}>Choose an option:</label>
      <input
        id={inputId}
        role="combobox"
        aria-expanded="false"
        aria-controls={listboxId}
        aria-autocomplete="list"
      />
      <ul id={listboxId} role="listbox">
        {options.map((option, index) => (
          <li key={option} id={`${baseId}-option-${index}`} role="option">
            {option}
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </div>
  );
}

This pattern creates a stable prefix that all related IDs share. The input gets ":r1:-input", the listbox gets ":r1:-listbox", and each option gets ":r1:-option-0", ":r1:-option-1", etc. The prefix never changes across renders, so ARIA relationships remain intact.

Developers sometimes call useId multiple times in the same component instead of concatenating suffixes. This works but generates longer IDs and slightly increases the risk of tree position collisions if the component structure changes. A single call with suffixes is more explicit about the relationship between the IDs.

For components that render in a loop, the key should come from the data (as discussed earlier), but the internal IDs can still use useId. Each instance of the component gets a unique useId result based on its position in the tree.

function FormFieldList({ fields }: { fields: FieldConfig[] }) {
  return (
    <>
      {fields.map((field) => (
        <FormField key={field.name} config={field} />
      ))}
    </>
  );
}

function FormField({ config }: { config: FieldConfig }) {
  const baseId = useId();
  const inputId = `${baseId}-input`;
  const hintId = `${baseId}-hint`;

  return (
    <div>
      <label htmlFor={inputId}>{config.label}</label>
      <input id={inputId} aria-describedby={hintId} />
      <p id={hintId}>{config.hint}</p>
    </div>
  );
}

This separation keeps keys tied to data (the field.name) while letting useId handle the internal ID generation for each field instance. The pattern described in building apps with React Hooks extends this to entire forms managed through custom Hooks.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I use useId to generate database record IDs?

No. useId generates IDs tied to the component's position in the React tree. These IDs change when the component unmounts and remounts, and they are not globally unique across different React trees or server instances. Database IDs require globally unique identifiers like UUIDs or auto-incrementing integers generated by the database itself.

Why does useId return a colon-prefixed string instead of a plain number?

The colon prefix (:r1:, :r2:) ensures the generated IDs cannot collide with developer-defined IDs. If useId returned "1" or "field-1", developers who manually assign id="1" elsewhere in the tree would create conflicts. The colon makes it visually distinct and prevents accidental collisions.

Does useId work with React.lazy and code splitting?

Yes. useId works correctly with dynamically imported components because React's tree structure includes lazily loaded components in the parent path. The ID remains stable as long as the component mounts in the same tree position after the code chunk loads.

Can I call useId conditionally or inside a loop?

No. useId is a Hook, so it must follow the Rules of Hooks. Call it only at the top level of your component or custom Hook, never inside conditionals, loops, or nested functions. If you need multiple IDs, call useId once and concatenate suffixes, or extract a separate component that calls useId internally.

What happens if the server and client trees do not match?

React logs a hydration mismatch warning and re-renders the component on the client. The useId result may differ between the server HTML and the re-rendered client DOM, breaking accessibility relationships temporarily until the client render completes. The useId documentation explicitly requires an identical component tree on the server and client for the Hook to work correctly.

Making Your React Apps Accessible and Hydration-Safe

The useId Hook eliminates an entire class of SSR bugs by making ID generation deterministic. Developers no longer need to choose between accessibility and server rendering, or build workarounds with useEffect and client-only state.

Production applications using Next.js, Remix, or custom SSR setups should audit all form components and accessibility relationships. Any hardcoded ID or Math.random() call in a server-rendered component is a hydration risk. Replacing them with useId costs nothing at runtime and prevents subtle bugs that only appear in production.

For teams building component libraries, useId should be the default for any internal ID generation. Expose the base ID through props if consumers need to reference it externally, but handle the generation internally. This pattern works across frameworks and server rendering strategies without requiring consumers to understand hydration mechanics.

The Hook is not a silver bullet. It does not replace data-derived keys, cache identifiers, or globally unique tokens. It solves one specific problem: generating stable, collision-free IDs for DOM elements within a React component tree. For that use case, it is the only correct solution in a server-rendered application.

articles.title: I built a racing sim that runs in a browser tab
articles.description: im racing usually starts with a big download and a decent PC. I wanted one you could open from a...
articles.body_html:
im racing usually starts with a big download and a decent PC. I wanted one you could open from a link.

That's LibreCorsa. It runs in the browser and it's open source. There are 2026-style open-wheelers, GT3s, a prototype and a road car, more than a dozen circuits, AI races, ghosts, rain and online races. You can drive it with a keyboard, a gamepad, a touch screen or a steering wheel. If you'd rather watch first, there's a 40-second trailer.

I'm building it on my own. It's a little over 800 commits since mid-October, and a few parts turned out much more interesting than I expected.

500 Hz, whatever your screen does

If the physics depends on frame rate, a 144 Hz monitor gives you more grip than a 60 Hz laptop. In a racing game you notice that within a lap.

So the simulation moves in fixed 2 ms steps (500 Hz), and each step splits into four 0.5 ms substeps for the tyres and suspension. The screen renders at whatever rate it can, and the sim catches up in whole steps. Stripped down, it's the classic loop:

const STEP = 0.002; // 500 Hz
let acc = 0;

function frame(dt: number) {
  acc = Math.min(acc + dt, 0.1); // a long hitch doesn't turn into a death spiral
  while (acc >= STEP) {
    sim.step(STEP); // four 0.5 ms substeps inside
    acc -= STEP;
  }
  render(sim.state);
}

One detail I didn't see coming: your steering input arrives once per frame, but a frame can run three physics steps or none. So each change is spread across the steps that frame actually runs, the way a real wheel turns, instead of landing all at once on the first one.

Does it hold? I run the same three-second launch at 30, 60, 144 and 240 fps, and the car ends within 0.3 km/h and 0.2 m every time. The test suite runs it at two frame rates and fails if they disagree.

Tyres are most of the work

The tyre is a Pacejka-style slip curve with combined slip, load sensitivity and carcass relaxation. Then it gets complicated. Each tyre tracks inner, middle and outer temperatures, and those move the grip window. Pressure follows the ideal gas law and changes how stiff the carcass is. Tyres wear. In the rain the road carries a water film that builds and drains, the cars dry the racing line first, and wets clear water up to a depth before they aquaplane.

The ground under the tyre mattered more than I thought. With one ground sample per wheel, a kerb's step edge gets hit at a point instead of rolled over. Each tyre now takes five samples across its contact patch (centre, both ends, both edges) and folds them into one height and slope.

There are two vehicle models. The default car has a planar chassis with sprung heave, pitch and roll. The others run a full 6-DOF rigid body with suspension built from hardpoints, so camber, bump steer and anti-dive come out of the geometry instead of numbers I typed in. On those cars the steering torque is the front tyres' moment about the kingpin axes. That's what a wheel actually pushes back with.

Checking it against a real car

When you're the only tester, tuning by feel only goes so far. I have about 24 minutes of MoTeC logs from a real GT3 Evo at Valencia, so the sim's GT3 runs the same manoeuvres: sustained cornering, braking and full-throttle acceleration at each speed, plus the gearing and the understeer gradient.

Right now every point sits within −13 % to +17 % of the logs. Not great, not terrible. The validation page is generated from the sim's own code with one command, and it has a section for where the sim is wrong. CI fails the build if a point leaves its band, and the last physics rework pushed one of them out.

Steering wheels in a browser

Steering, pedals and buttons were the easy part. If your OS sees the wheel as a game controller, the Gamepad API sees it too.

Force feedback is not easy. Chrome and Edge have WebHID, so a page can talk to a wheel base directly, and bases that speak the standard USB HID PID force-feedback reports can be driven with nothing installed. Plenty of popular wheels don't speak it. Logitech's force feedback is proprietary, for one. For those there's a small Windows helper that talks DirectInput and listens on localhost.

Where it stands: the one wheel I've tested, a MOZA R9, connects and steers over WebHID, but I haven't confirmed force feedback on it yet. It's marked experimental. If you have a different wheel, there's a wheel report form on GitHub and I'd love to see it filled in.

Racing people without paying for servers

Multiplayer is peer-to-peer over WebRTC. You host a room and send the link, or a friend types a 6-character code. If you want zero servers, there's a manual offer/answer copy-paste with nothing in between. Two tabs on the same machine can also race each other, which made testing a lot less lonely.

On the live site a small Cloudflare Worker does the rest. It pairs players, hands out relay servers for networks that block a direct link, keeps the leaderboards, and starts an open race every 20 minutes on the week's circuit and car. If nobody shows up, you race the AI.

Half a gigabyte, hosted for free

The game is a static Next.js export on Cloudflare, which is great until a circuit model is bigger than the asset store's 25 MiB per-file limit. Those files sit in an R2 bucket instead. The Worker answers any path that has no static file from R2, at the same URL, so the game never knows.

Car models are meshopt-compressed when the site builds. The default car drops from 16 MB to 6 MB, which matters when the first thing a player sees is a loading screen.

Hosting costs nothing at the moment. I'd like to keep it that way.

Licences, and why the repo is small

The code is MIT. The 3D models and sounds come from a lot of different authors with their own licences, and some are non-commercial. So LibreCorsa has no ads and nothing for sale. There's a Buy Me a Coffee link and that's it.

It's also why the repository carries only one circuit, RISE Motordrome, and the 2026 prototype car. Everything else is served on the site for playing there. A clone still gives you a working game with those two, and there's a guide for porting your own cars locally.

What's rough

VR works through WebXR, but it's a work in progress. Force feedback in the browser is experimental. Circuits converted from community 3D models have less trustworthy surfaces than the hand-built ones. And the handling is tuned by one person, which is exactly why I want other people driving it.

Try it

It's at librecorsa.org, and the code is on GitHub. Tell me how it drives, especially on a gamepad or a wheel I don't have, and how it runs on your machine.

LibreCorsa is an independent fan project. It isn't affiliated with Formula 1, the FIA, or any team or circuit.

articles.title: I put twelve 3D guests on our wedding website instead of writing "smart casual" (no 3D library)
articles.description: Shani and I get married in March 2027, in the highlands of South Africa. Every wedding website I...
articles.body_html:
Shani and I get married in March 2027, in the highlands of South Africa. Every wedding website I looked at had the same dress-code section: a line that says "smart casual" and leaves everyone guessing.

So I built ours by hand, and on the "What to wear" page I put twelve guests instead of a sentence.

boomslangchips.github.io

They show what to wear on each day of the weekend. They breathe, shift their weight, look around, fold their arms, glance at each other. You can drag one to turn them round, tap to step closer, and try the wedding colours on them.

There is no game engine and no 3D library behind it: about 250 KB of plain JavaScript and WebGL 1, plus one 760 KB file for the bodies. It runs on a phone.

How it fits together

File What it does
atelier-core.js Vectors, matrices, mesh building (tubes, shells, patches) and the WebGL renderer: skin, cloth, knit, denim, satin and hair shaders, a soft shadow map, the floor's reflection
atelier-body.js Reads the MakeHuman base mesh (CC0) in three body shapes, 163 bones and skin weights, and poses a body
atelier-cloth.js A small position-based cloth simulation for skirts and long hair, kept out of the body by the body's own cross-sections
atelier-figure.js One guest: body, face, hair, every garment cut round that body, shoes, accessories, and the arm poses
atelier-stage.js The stage: day tabs, dragging, the colour swatches, and each guest's little "mind" (breath, weight shifts, glances, blinks, smiles)

The hardest part was hands

Rendering was not the hard bit. Hands were.

A hand "on the hip" that floats a centimetre away looks wrong instantly. One that sinks into the hip looks worse. Folded hands that pass through each other are the first thing anyone notices. So each resting pose is solved: two-bone IK for the arm, then a small solver that places the palm against the surface it rests on, for every body shape.

The stage also watches its own frame time and does less on slow devices, and nothing moves at all if you have reduced motion turned on.

Honest limits

  • The guests stand in place: no walking.
  • Fingers keep one relaxed shape.
  • Creases at elbows and knees are drawn on the cloth, not simulated.
  • All faces are variations of one head.

The rest of the site

Our real site is private (it has our guest list on it), so I made a twin with a made-up couple and stock photos that you can click through: the invitation gate, a countdown, the weekend day by day, a drawn venue map, where to stay, an RSVP that knows who is on each invitation, and add-to-calendar.

👉 Demo: https://demo.wentzel.wedding (the invitation code is DEMO)
👉 3D guests, MIT licence: https://github.com/BoomslangChips/wedding-guests-3d

I wrote it with Claude Code over a few very long days. Happy to answer how any part works in the comments.

articles.title: I put a real LLM in my portfolio. It runs on your GPU, not my server.
articles.description: In-browser RAG with WebLLM and WebGPU, a hero animation that fires with every token, and the four mistakes I fixed on the way to Lighthouse 100.
articles.body_html:
Every AI-engineer portfolio says "I build with LLMs." I wanted mine to prove it in the first ten seconds.

So the chat box on my homepage has a button: Run a real LLM on your GPU. Click it and a 0.5B-parameter model downloads into your browser, boots on your graphics card through WebGPU, and answers questions about my work. No server. No API key. Nothing you type leaves your machine.

👉 Try it: rahul-agarwal.in (desktop Chrome or Edge works best)

Here's how it works, and the four things I got wrong before it worked well.

What happens when you click the button

  1. The page checks for WebGPU and whether your GPU supports 16-bit floats.
  2. It lazy-loads WebLLM from a CDN (none of this code ships until you ask for it).
  3. It downloads Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (about 270 MB, 4-bit quantised). Your browser caches it, so the second visit is instant.
  4. Every question runs a tiny retrieval step over my notes, then the model answers using only what was retrieved.
  5. Each generated token fires a pulse through the animated neural network behind the hero, so you can literally watch it think.

Loading the model (the part that's easier than you'd expect) 

const adapter = await navigator.gpu.requestAdapter();
const f16 = adapter.features.has('shader-f16');
const model = f16
  ? 'Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct-q4f16_1-MLC'
  : 'Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct-q4f32_1-MLC'; // fallback for GPUs without fp16

const webllm = await import('https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@mlc-ai/web-llm@0.2.86/+esm');
const engine = await webllm.CreateMLCEngine(model, {
  initProgressCallback: r => updateProgressBar(r.progress, r.text),
});

That's it. WebLLM exposes an OpenAI-style API, so streaming looks familiar:

const chunks = await engine.chat.completions.create({
  messages, stream: true, temperature: 0.2, max_tokens: 160,
});
for await (const c of chunks) {
  const token = c.choices[0]?.delta?.content || '';
  output.textContent += token;
  window.neural.fire(1); // light up the hero network
}

Two details matter: pin the CDN version (an unpinned import can change under you), and check for shader-f16 instead of assuming it. Plenty of laptop GPUs don't have it.

Grounding a 0.5B model with a 30-line RAG

A half-billion-parameter model knows nothing about me and will happily invent things. So it never answers from memory. Every question goes through a retrieval step first:

// Simplified from the real code, which also weights longer keywords higher
function retrieve(question) {
  const q = question.toLowerCase();
  return NOTES
    .map(note => ({ note, score: note.keys.filter(k => q.includes(k)).length }))
    .filter(x => x.score > 0)
    .sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score)
    .slice(0, 2)
    .map(x => x.note);
}

const SYSTEM = `Answer in 1 to 3 short sentences using ONLY the notes provided.
If the notes don't contain the answer, say you don't know.
Never invent companies, numbers, dates or links.`;

The notes are a dozen short paragraphs I wrote (projects, stack, experience). Keyword scoring sounds crude next to embeddings, but with a dozen documents it's instant, deterministic and easy to debug. Under every answer the UI shows what it used:

Q: Where does he work now?
A: Rahul is the sole engineer at Aryan News Agency, where he builds and develops websites and apps.
↳ retrieved 1 note (intro) · 22 tokens in 2.8s · generated on your GPU

And the test I cared about most:

Q: What is his favourite food?
A: Rahul is not specifically known for his favorite food.

No hallucination. Low temperature plus a strict "only the notes" prompt does most of the work.

Four things I got wrong

1. The first answer took 28 seconds

The model loaded fine, but the first question sat there "thinking." WebGPU compiles its shaders lazily, on the first real inference. The fix is a throwaway warm-up generation while the progress bar is still visible:

await engine.chat.completions.create({
  messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Hi' }], max_tokens: 4,
});

Now the slow part happens during loading, where users expect waiting, not after they've asked a question.

2. A text animation wrecked my layout score

My headline "decodes" from random glyphs into the real text. It looked great, and it gave the page a Cumulative Layout Shift of 1.41 (anything above 0.25 is "poor"). Random glyphs have different widths, so the line re-wrapped about 60 times a second and shoved everything below it around.

The fix: wrap each word in an inline-block, lock it to its real width, scramble inside it, then unwrap.

for (const w of words) {
  w.span.style.display = 'inline-block';
  w.span.style.width = w.span.getBoundingClientRect().width + 'px';
}
// ...animate...then restore plain text nodes
words.forEach(w => w.span.replaceWith(document.createTextNode(w.text)));

Same effect, layout shift 0.00. One more catch: measure after document.fonts.ready, or you lock in the fallback font's widths.

3. My CDN was editing my HTML

I added a strict Content-Security-Policy (hash-based, no unsafe-inline). Locally: zero violations. In production: errors. My domain was proxied through Cloudflare in front of Vercel, and Cloudflare was injecting its own inline scripts (analytics and bot detection) and rewriting my email address into an obfuscated link. That put an <a> inside my "copy email" <button>.

Switching the DNS records to "DNS only" removed the extra hop and the rewriting. The strict CSP went back on, and the page got faster. If you put a CDN in front of a platform that's already a CDN, check what it's adding to your pages.

4. Assuming everyone has WebGPU

Plenty of visitors (many phones, older browsers) can't run the model. The chat works without it: by default it streams pre-written answers token by token, clearly labelled as "scripted mode". The real model is opt-in, behind an explicit button that shows the download size. Nobody gets a 270 MB surprise on mobile data.

The numbers

Framework none: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript
HTML + CSS + JS over the wire ~37 KB gzipped
Lighthouse (desktop) 100 / 100 / 100 / 100
Lighthouse (mobile) 97 / 100 / 100 / 100
Mozilla Observatory A+
Model download (optional) ~270 MB once, then cached

No React, no build step. Every heavy thing (the model, the runtime) loads only when someone asks for it, and every animation pauses when it scrolls off screen.

What I'd do differently

  • A 0.5B model is a demo, not a product. It's grounded and fast, but its phrasing is sometimes clumsy. With a bigger download budget, a 1.5B model is noticeably better.
  • Keyword retrieval doesn't scale. Past a few dozen notes I'd switch to small embeddings computed in the browser.
  • First load is the real UX problem. On a slow connection the download takes minutes. The progress bar helps, but caching the model with a service worker before anyone clicks would be smarter.

Have you shipped anything that runs a model fully client-side? I'd love to hear what you used and what broke. Drop it in the comments 👇

I'm Rahul, an AI engineer in Bengaluru who builds tools that ship. More of my work is at rahul-agarwal.in, and the code is on GitHub.

articles.title: I Built a Free Browser Shooter Set in a Pakistani Old-City Bazaar
articles.description: A free desktop-browser shooter set in Purana Shehr, a Pakistani old-city bazaar. What's in the game, what it needs, and how to try it.
articles.body_html:
I built a shooter set in a Pakistani bazaar, and it runs in a desktop browser. There is nothing to install.

The game is called Operation Androon. A match is 8 v 8 team deathmatch against computer-controlled soldiers, and the first team to 50 eliminations wins. The map is Purana Shehr: an old-city bazaar with a clock tower, shop signs in Urdu, decorated trucks, rickshaws, fruit stalls, and a haveli courtyard.

I am a lead full-stack engineer in Lahore, and the founder of MyLeadBots. On my site, azeemshafeeq.com, I describe these games as side projects where I learn game development. Androon is one of them. This post is a clear look at what is in the game, what it needs, and what it is not.

The place: Purana Shehr

Purana Shehr is a fictional Pakistani old-city bazaar. The name is Urdu for "old city," and the map is built around details you would expect to see in that kind of place, not around a generic arena with a different coat of paint.

The square is marked by a clock tower. Shop signs are in Urdu. Decorated trucks sit in the lanes. There are rickshaws, fruit stalls, and a haveli courtyard. Lanes are narrow enough that a firefight can move from the street into a doorway and then up a stairwell.

You can go inside buildings, climb the stairs, and fight from the rooftops. That matters for how a match feels. A rooftop gives you a line of sight over the bazaar; a shop interior gives you cover and a tighter fight. The map plays as a small district: streets, interiors, and rooftops, not a flat deathmatch pad.

Civilians shelter in the shops. Hitting one costs your team points. The bazaar is not only scenery. If you spray through a storefront, you can lose ground even if you win the gunfight.

I will not call the graphics photorealistic, and I will not call them console-quality. This is a browser game, built for the web, and the honest description is that it is a stylized place you can move through, not a simulation of a real street.

How a match works

A match is straightforward:

  • You play 8 v 8, on a team, alongside and against bots.
  • The first team to 50 eliminations wins.
  • Eight weapons unlock as you get kills.
  • Grenades are in the mix, and a 5-kill streak calls in an airstrike.
  • You can switch between first-person and third-person views.

The bots are the other team and your teammates. I am not calling this multiplayer. You are not dropping into a match with other people over the network. You are playing a team deathmatch against computer-controlled soldiers in your browser.

The weapon unlocks give the match a short arc. You start with less, and you earn more as you get kills. The airstrike on a 5-kill streak is a payoff for a run that stays clean. None of that changes the basic rule: first to 50.

There is also a Veteran difficulty, if you want a harder pass through the same map.

First-person and third-person are both there because the bazaar rewards both ways of looking. First-person is tighter in a doorway or on a stair. Third-person makes it easier to see the edge of a rooftop or the corner of a lane before you step into it. You can switch as you play.

If you have played classic military shooters, the loop will feel familiar: a team deathmatch, a small set of weapons, a map you learn by running it. Operation Androon is an original game. The setting is the part worth naming clearly: a Pakistani old-city bazaar, not a stand-in for somewhere else.

What it runs on, and what it does not

Operation Androon is free. It runs in a desktop browser. There is no download and nothing to install.

It needs a laptop or PC with a mouse and keyboard. It does not work on phones. I am stating that up front because a browser game is easy to open on a phone, and this one will not play well there. The controls assume a mouse and a keyboard.

The first load is about 42 MB. On a new device, or a slower connection, that first visit can take a moment. After that, you are in the bazaar.

Those limits are worth stating clearly, not hiding in a footnote. A desktop browser can hold a small 3D district, interiors, and a team of bots. A phone screen and a touch overlay are a different game, and this is not that game.

Where this sits in my work

Most of my professional work is web and AI products. MyLeadBots is a SaaS tool I built for small web agencies and freelance website builders: it finds local businesses from Google Maps, checks their public presence, and prepares reviewable proof before a pitch. I also ship other production work, which I keep on azeemshafeeq.com.

The games are how I learn a different kind of building. Androon is the bazaar shooter. Next to it I have been working on Morrow, a 3D night-city district that also runs in a desktop browser, and Sands of the Lost Kingdom, a fantasy adventure whose first chapter is a macOS preview built in Godot. I am not packing those into this article. I mention them only so the context is honest: Androon is a side project, and it is one of a small set.

I am writing this as a show-and-tell, not as a launch with user numbers or a claim about how it plays for other people. I have not published player counts, scores, or reviews, and I will not invent any here.

Credit

The soldier model is "PAKISTAN soldier – PAK ARMY" by Abdullah5007 on Sketchfab, licensed under CC BY 4.0, then rigged and modified for the game. The licence requires attribution, so I am putting it here in the article as well as on my site.

If you want to try it

If you want to play Operation Androon, DM me on X @azeem_sh123 and I will send the link. Use a laptop or PC with a mouse and keyboard.

I would rather hear what you notice about the map than a generic "cool game" note. The useful feedback is specific: a lane that is hard to read, a rooftop that works, a shop you expected to be able to enter, a Pakistani detail that is missing.

If you were adding one thing to a bazaar map like this, what would you put in next: another street, another weapon, or something quieter, like a tea stall you can actually walk into?

articles.title: Keep client customisations out of your product: an iframe sandbox
articles.description: Every client wants something different, and AI makes it cheap to build. I built a zero-dependency browser sandbox so those customisations stay out of
articles.body_html:
Every client wants something slightly different, and AI just made those differences cheap to build. I think that changes how products get shaped, so I built a sandbox for it: sandbox-environment, Apache-2.0, zero runtime dependencies, on JSR as @panth977/sandbox.

I'm Panth Patel. I work on backends and developer tooling, and this is the argument behind the library more than a tour of it.

From product to framework

Many companies went from solutions to SaaS: stop building one thing per client and sell one thing to everyone. My view is that the next move runs from product to framework. With AI around, and with less organised sectors coming online, each client will have different needs and will expect them met.

Those needs have to live somewhere. The easy answer is to have AI stitch them into your app. It works for a while. Then your product code holds every client's special case, and each customisation is a product change with a product release.

The better principle is a line. Framework code on one side, client customisation on the other, and a sandbox as that line. Yes, you'll probably still use AI to write what goes inside it. That is fine. What changes is where the code lands.

It gives you two things. A customisation that needs no product code change can ship in hours instead of weeks. And if the client has a tech team of their own, you can hand them the sandbox and let them maintain it.

What it looks like

A customisation is an artifact: a mini-app mounted in a slot of your app.

import { mount, scopes, confirm, audit } from "jsr:@panth977/sandbox/host";

mount(document.getElementById("slot")!, {
  artifact,
  api: {
    devices: {
      list: (q) => http.get("/devices", { params: q }),   // uses YOUR token
    },
  },
  middleware: [
    audit((e) => log.push(e)),
    scopes({ "devices.list": "devices:read" }, granted),
  ],
});

Inside the artifact, the code only sees the API you passed in:

import { host } from "@panth977/sandbox/artifact";
const rows = await host.devices.list();

Your frontend is its backend. The call crosses a typed bridge, runs in your app with the viewer's permissions, and comes back. Streams, callbacks, cancellation and errors cross it too.

Where the boundary comes from

I didn't write a security model. I used the browser's. Each artifact runs in an <iframe sandbox="allow-scripts"> with an opaque origin, so it has no access to your DOM, cookies, localStorage or tokens. A strict CSP closes the network unless the artifact's manifest asks and the host allows it. Scopes, confirm-before-destructive, rate limits, an audit trail and dry runs are middleware, a line each.

The threat model is written down in SECURITY.md. The artifact is untrusted, and the host and its API are trusted. Two things are out of scope: an artifact wasting its own frame, and anything your API chooses to allow. The sandbox stops the code from reaching around your API. You still have to design that API with care.

Writing artifacts in the browser

A sandbox nobody can write for doesn't help. So the package includes the tools:

  • A compiler that takes TypeScript, JSX and Svelte in the browser or a worker, with no bundler and no WASM. The same compiler runs in Node for CI.
  • mountDev: a Monaco editor with completions and go-to-definition, plus a live preview.
  • A UI kit, so artifacts look like part of your app.

Hosts can be plain JS, Svelte or Angular, tested in CI in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, with Angular as far back as 15. Artifacts can be plain JS, React, Preact or Svelte 5. A React host should work through the custom element, but I haven't tested one in a real React app yet.

What's next

This release covers the frontend. The next one is a backend sandbox: write the code in any language, while the host keeps full control over the script and its security.

Where do client customisations live in your product today?
